    Seven required simulations¶

    Simulation Concrete walkthrough and improvement Result and required local checks
    1. Grade 3 substitute arrives 20 minutes before class Bridge Engineering has a 40-minute sequence, background, fair-test directions, individual evidence and cleanup. The handoff supplies a 20-minute prep gate. Integration corrected its mismatch with the generic nine-team kit: budget 13 kits for 12 active teams at 25, 26 books, 260 counters, 28 sheets and 5.2 m tape. Conditional document pass: feasible with the prepared counted kit. Actual location, supplies, room, accommodations and pretest must be confirmed. Otherwise use the explicitly different fallback and record deferred objectives.
    2. Kindergarten child cannot read Movement/picture algorithms uses modeled arrows, large paper pieces, pointing/moving and oral evidence; Show, Try, Tell supports nonwritten responses. Document pass for the reference pathway: independent reading/handwriting is not required. The teacher still checks each child's reasoning and gives the third child a full turn.
    3. iPads unavailable Technology plan and actual lesson alternatives separate computational reasoning from digital execution. Current labels: 149 None, 49 Optional, 15 Recommended, 38 Required. Approved Snap/protected-AA circuit routes need no computing device but retain physical-material gates. Conditional program pass: the documented low-tech core continues. Real programming, robot/sensor operation and digital-tool objectives requiring devices are deferred, not falsely awarded from paper or teacher demonstration.
    4. Minnesota January, -10 F K picture grids/indoor observation, paper bridge tests, the indoor weather reference and fictional paper evidence require no outdoor exposure. Prepared/simulated data are labeled. Document pass for selected indoor pathways: authentic outdoor measurements cannot be claimed from simulated data; move or explicitly change such objectives. Live plant care and indoor wet-work cleanup need local planning.
    5. Enrollment rises to 25 Exact reference tables, roles, seated testing and individual roster sweeps replace serial queues. Generic groups <=3 need nine kits; pair-based references retain larger budgets. The selected Snap routes use nine teams/five stations/two waves within the native meeting. Conditional capacity pass: arithmetic and written logistics cover 25. Use the exact selected pathway, not a universal kit count. Physical space, stock, inspection throughput and observed individual turns remain untested.
    6. Limited funding Starter plan totals $229.52 with supplies, tax/shipping/contingency estimates and no required devices, specialty loans or donations. Existing school basics and one-cohort consumables are explicit. Conditional budget pass: prices/specifications and stock are estimates. This is a modest low-tech core, not purchase coverage for all 251 legacy lessons or all pair-based references. Safe electrical procurement may not be improvised to preserve a price.
    7. Parent asks what the child learns Family system, band unit snippets, scope, progression and traceability connect concepts/actions, Catholic reasoning, planned evidence and next steps. The forensic reference makes truth/dignity concrete without accusing anyone. Document pass: a teacher can explain a selected lesson and its progression in plain language. Describe actual evidence gathered; never imply that planned targets or group participation prove mastery. Home invitations are optional.

    Weaknesses exposed and corrected during integration¶

    1. Unit totals had been stored as per-meeting minutes in some audits. All rows now use native 25/30/40/45 minutes; meetings * minutes gives duration.
    2. Shared substitute guidance used a nine-team kit for a pair-based bridge. The handoff now uses the exact conservative 13-kit supply budget.
    3. Protected AA circuits were inconsistently counted as requiring digital technology. Labels now distinguish digital needs from required physical materials; electrical mastery still requires an actual safely tested circuit.
    4. A Grades 1-2 bridge table needed an explicit odd-enrollment arrangement. A final trio and reserve kit are specified, with individual role rotation.
    5. Outside-document script links in band reviews were replaced with the published traceability guide and an inline command.
    6. The operations snapshot was stale after lesson revisions. Materials and technology summaries now use the integrated audit counts and generated maps.
    7. Exact-name material matching exposed unresolved terms. They remain visible for reconciliation; no invented quantities, prices or equivalent items are silently supplied.

    Remaining release conditions¶

    The band reviews record unresolved instructional/source/operational holds. An improved file is not a full reference rebuild; a full document is not a classroom certification. Hold unresolved P0 pathways and finish the next scheduled P1 lesson before teaching.

    Before calling the program uniformly classroom-ready, confirm actual stock, protected electrical specifications, supplier prices, school safety/privacy/ account rules, accommodations, source-gated history/Church claims, applicable official benchmark mapping and physical kit locations. Pilot scheduled lessons, time preparation/cleanup, gather individual evidence on the local mastery checkpoints and revise using those observations.

    K has zero remaining document-package holds. Its physical/school/source gates and classroom trials remain; the other three bands' documented readiness queues were not silently closed by the autonomous K work.

    Initial evidence, not conclusions about every lesson¶

    • A Kindergarten robotics unit requires charged, paired robots and iPads. Direction, prediction and sequencing can also be taught physically; actual robot-operation objectives must remain distinct from an unplugged fallback.
    • A Grades 1-2 bridge session labels a papal bridge metaphor as Scripture. That attribution is inaccurate and needs correction, not repetition.
    • A Grades 3-4 bridge lesson includes efficiency ratios without establishing whether those calculations fit the younger grade's prerequisites.
    • A Grades 5-6 forensic session leaves sample preparation, "safe" unknown substances and fictional evidence unspecified. A substitute needs a complete, non-accusatory investigation with no unknown powders or real student profiling.
    • The general substitute guide asks for a quick-reference card without proving that such a card exists for every activity.
    • Home, planning and template pages emphasize digital art. Art also needs purposeful observational drawing, model design, pattern, composition and communication without a device.
    • Materials guidance mixes classroom basics with specialty robots, loan kits and apps. Availability, quantities, annual consumables and minimum operating cost must be separated.

    Audit method and change policy¶

    Four grade-band workstreams inspect every lesson, record baseline findings, and make targeted improvements before publishing their audit. A separate standards workstream verifies authoritative sources. Program integration uses these records rather than inferring alignment from lesson titles or tags.

    The internal mapping is grade -> rotation/schedule -> unit -> lesson -> demonstrated skills/local standards -> materials -> assessment. Evidence records distinguish original quality from the revision state.

    Audit dispositions are KEEP, KEEP + IMPROVE, REBUILD, REPLACE and REMOVE. No file is deleted merely because an alternative is preferred. Recommendations retain useful activities and identify safety, accuracy and substitute-readiness issues first.

    Quality uses four evidence levels: 0 absent/unsafe, 1 named but underspecified, 2 teachable with a specific support or remaining check, 3 explicit and independently usable. Dimensions include academic rigor, developmental fit, Catholic integration, standards evidence, hands-on engagement, instruction/substitute clarity, low-tech access, cost/preparation, assessment, inclusion, safety, scalability, family communication and progression. Scores are editorial judgments, not classroom-outcome measurements.

    Verification limits: A document review cannot certify actual school inventory, individual accommodations, equipment condition, classroom outcomes, diocesan approval or complete coverage of the primary subject curricula. Unverified official benchmarks are marked VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    Getting Started

    C-STREAM quick start guide¶

    October 2026. C = Catholic identity; S = science; T = technology; R = religion/faith integration; E = engineering; A = arts including music; M = mathematics. Catholic purpose shapes choices, not only opening prayer. Art involves observation, composition, form, pattern or communication, not just decoration/digital tools.

    Before the first meeting¶

    1. Confirm weekly/bi-weekly schedule and A/B rotation with the school. Use the lesson index; do not assume the same Week 1 filename or commercial-kit schedule for every band.
    2. Read the actual lesson objective, background, vocabulary, safety, individual check and timed sequence. Use the common lesson format.
    3. Confirm supplies and location with inventory checklist. Default 10/15/20/25 pupils = ⅘/7/9 teams <=3. School provides required supplies.
    4. Perform the teacher pretest and count trays. Have the substitute fallback ready.
    5. Prepare family copy. No routine homework.
    Grade Native period Protect inside this time
    K 25 minutes Oral modeling, each child's action/evidence, 3-minute cleanup
    1-2 30 minutes Hands-on turns/test/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup
    3-4 40 minutes Evidence-based testing/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup
    5-6 45 minutes Reasoning/tradeoffs, individual check, 4-minute cleanup

    Your first two weeks¶

    Start with a completed band lesson, not a generic untimed welcome sequence. Model "notice -> try -> tell"; nonreader card. State "Today I can..." and give every child a turn to show the objective. Next meeting, use observation/design/measurement appropriate to prerequisites. Failure in engineering is information, not failure of a student.

    If a source question arises, say "We need to check that" and record VERIFICATION REQUIRED. The Catholic heritage guide is background for source checking, not a mandatory biography every lesson. No internet image search, unlicensed image or unverified quotation is needed.

    If conditions change¶

    • Time short: stop new construction; keep individual evidence and cleanup.
    • Kit absent: use the named safe fallback, recording any objective change.
    • Devices absent: unplugged concepts still work; real programming/robot execution evidence must be deferred, not claimed from drawings.
    • Unsafe materials/weather: stop and use a seated indoor task; notify the responsible school adult if safety needs escalation.

    Next links: materials plan, technology plan, assessment, FAQ, differentiation, templates.

    Parent Quick Explanations¶

    What is C-STREAM?

    C-STREAM stands for Catholic Science, Technology, Religion, Engineering, Art & Music, and Mathematics. It's like STEM, but with Catholic faith woven throughout. Your child learns that faith and science work together to understand God's amazing world.

    Why Catholic STEM?

    Catholic education has always valued both faith and reason. We help students see that the same God who inspired the Psalms also created the laws of physics. Learning about creation helps us know and love the Creator.

    How can I help at home?

    Ask questions! Show curiosity about what your child is learning. Point out science and engineering in everyday life. Wonder aloud about how things work. Most importantly, help your child see God in the amazing world around them.

    ✅ Assessment & Progress¶

    Evidence of learning, not participation percentages¶

    Evidence What to assess
    Individual oral explanation, drawing or demonstration The stated science, mathematics, computing or design objective
    Test record and revision Whether the student uses evidence to explain an improvement
    Ethical or stewardship choice An age-appropriate reason about people/resources, not the child's personal piety
    Collaboration and effort Record separately from mastery; successful group work does not prove every student's understanding

    Use a simple objective-linked rubric and the local progression. Do not grade handwriting, artistic polish or reading proficiency unless it is the actual objective.

    Progress Tracking¶

    Each trimester, assess: - [ ] STEM skill development - [ ] Faith integration understanding - [ ] Collaboration growth - [ ] Wonder and curiosity cultivation

    C-STREAM FAQ and troubleshooting¶

    October 2026. Start with Quick Start and a completed lesson template. Generalist teachers can teach a clear lesson; not every legacy file is ready. Confirm rotation/calendar and the actual lesson rather than promising no repetition or universal substitute-readiness.

    Time and classroom management¶

    Running long? Stop new construction, retain the individual check and cleanup, store dry labeled work and continue next meeting. Do not delete evidence collection to add an extra activity or prayer.

    Finished early? Ask for a repeated fair test, alternative constraint or explanation of evidence. Faster pupils are not automatically unpaid helpers.

    Students excited/arguing? Give instructions before materials, use a stop signal, assign builder/tester/reporter and rotate actual turns. Ask each to show an idea and test alternatives under the same conditions. Refer persistent behavior/safety concerns through actual school procedures.

    A child needs more time? Model one step, reduce choices, pre-cut/larger materials, allow gesture/voice/scribe/quiet or seated response. Keep the concept criterion unless documenting an explicit objective change.

    Missing supplies or technology¶

    Problem Safe response Learning limit
    Building blocks absent Paper/cardstock/sticks with a stated new constraint Compare evidence; do not silently claim identical load capacity
    Robot/app/host unavailable Desk-grid arrow cards and pointer Sequence/debugging concepts only; execution/robot mastery deferred
    Internet absent Teacher-vetted read-aloud source or confirmed offline tool Actual online/source-navigation objective may change
    Some devices work Document turn/reset time, smaller test rotations or more meetings Each child needs individual real-device evidence if that is O1
    Electrical gear damaged Switch off/disconnect; OUT OF SERVICE; safe paper-path model Paper path is not practical circuit-building mastery
    No safe materials or weather Seated observation fallback Record actual observation objective, not unperformed investigation

    Do not open personal accounts, install unapproved apps, bypass safeguards or improvise power supplies. Technology Plan. Borrowing lead times/fees/stock are VERIFICATION REQUIRED, not guaranteed two-week free access. Library planning.

    Assessment¶

    How do I grade? Use the objective -> prompt -> success condition -> individual evidence chain. Project rubric. Participation, effort, handwriting, neatness and confidence are not mastery. An artistic criterion is used only for an explicit arts objective.

    What if the model fails? A child can still explain valid evidence and redesign. A successful team model does not prove each member understands. NE means not yet evidenced; unobserved/absent/device-blocked is not a zero.

    How much paperwork? Short roster evidence during work plus one exit check; review termly with Progress Tracker. Named records/photos follow verified school privacy/consent practice; do not assume a digital account or public portfolio.

    Faith, arts and grade differences¶

    Faith connection feels forced? Use a concrete Catholic decision about dignity, truth, stewardship or service. R identifies the explicit reflection. Prayer supports but does not substitute for this purpose. Verify Church quotations, biographies and standards; never make an experiment theological proof.

    Hard science/faith question? Acknowledge uncertainty, distinguish observation from belief/interpretation and consult the verified source record or appropriate school faith educator. Avoid a simplistic "science only how, faith only why" rule or "God is an engineer" analogy.

    What does A mean? Arts including music: observational drawing, composition, visual communication, form, rhythmic phrases and performance, not just digital art/decoration. M means mathematics.

    K cannot read? Use Show, Try, Tell. An attempt is welcome but does not automatically demonstrate the concept. Assess pointing/sorting/building/telling with the same explicit success condition.

    Mixed grades / older students need challenge? Same materials can support different evidence expectations; use the shared progression and actual prerequisites. Add repeat trials, constraints, measurement or tradeoffs, not untaught ratio work or leadership as a substitute for subject learning.

    Safety and families¶

    No button cells, latex balloons or projectiles in the core; no neodymium magnets in K. Stop unsafe activities, isolate hazards and contact the school's responsible adult. Possible battery/magnet ingestion needs urgent emergency escalation. Use indoor alternatives in unsafe Minnesota conditions.

    No routine homework, required donations or home purchase/device. Explain concept + action + evidence + Catholic choice using family communication.

    🔄 Curriculum Flexibility Options¶

    C-STREAM offers flexible scheduling to meet your school's needs:

    Year A / Year B Rotation (Grades 1-6)¶

    For schools with combined grade classrooms (1-2, 3-4, 5-6), we provide a two-year rotation:

    • Year A: Complete curriculum with one set of projects and contexts

    • Year B: Same skills and concepts with different projects, saints, and applications

    Core competencies intentionally recur with increasing independence. Contexts vary, but the grade reviews identify actual overlaps and prerequisites. Kindergarten does not require Year A/B since students advance to 1st grade.

    • Weekly (34 calendar slots): Check multi-week meetings and holidays against the grade review; this is not 34 lesson files.

    • Bi-Weekly (17 sessions): Condensed curriculum for schools with STREAM every other week

    Review and readiness¶

    See the Kindergarten review and complete 37-row audit. Weekly and bi-weekly are alternative schedules, not lessons to combine into one year. Existing URLs remain unchanged.

    All 20 weekly documents are now complete instructional references after the autonomous closeout. Use the K teacher/substitute routines and the actual lesson's quantities and checks. This is document readiness, not physical-kit approval or classroom certification.

The source-verified arts candidates remain subject to MDE-copy/school review; exact science/math alignment and Archdiocesan approval are not implied. CST codes are local.

    📋 Kindergarten Pacing Notes¶

    📚 Materials Overview¶

    Minimum reusable classroom supplies (availability must be checked)¶

    • Paper, crayons, large picture/arrow cards and teacher-drawn grids

    • Ordinary wooden blocks or KEVA: up to 260 blocks for 25 pupils

    • Flashlights with secured battery compartments: up to 13 pair kits plus teacher light

    • Smooth cardboard, paper cups, tape, glue sticks and large paper shapes

    • Individual drawing/dictation records; enclosed adult-managed seed cups

    Optional additions; no checkout or class-set device prerequisite¶

    • One Dash/tablet or Sphero/tablet for teacher-controlled demonstrations or supervised real-hardware evidence

    🎯 Kindergarten Learning Goals¶

    By the end of the year, kindergarten students will be able to:

    STEM Skills¶

    • Follow a simple design process (think, plan, create, test)

    • Explain tool input/output and test picture algorithms; real robot operation/programming only when individually demonstrated

    • Make observations about the natural world

    • Build simple structures and test them

    • Recognize patterns in math and nature

    Faith Integration¶

    • Understand that learning about the world helps us know God better

    • Practice gratitude for God's creation

    • Show kindness and help others through STREAM work

    • Wonder at the beauty and order of creation

    21st Century Skills¶

    • Work cooperatively with a partner

    • Share ideas with the class

    • Try again when something doesn't work

    • Ask questions about how things work

    Grade Level: Kindergarten
    Framework: C-STREAM
    Last Updated: October 2026 (Kindergarten-only review)

    Week 1: Welcome to C-STREAM¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Welcome and observation / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea S, A; a detail we notice is different from a question we want to investigate
    Student objective / why "I can show a detail and ask a question." Scientists begin by noticing and wondering.
    Catholic connection Wonder at creation and respectful listening; use the source guidance in the routines below.
    Local standards CST-S1: observed detail/question; CST-A3: picture/oral communication. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 minutes included

    Before class and exact materials¶

    Read K routines. Make 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits at 10/15/20/25 pupils. Draw one large leaf with visible branching lines on each kit's half-sheet. Alternatively use an adult-inspected clean large leaf; pictures avoid allergies.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: large leaf drawing 5 8 10 13
    Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer, roster, crayon and one demonstration drawing reused from a kit. No letter cards, slideshow, purchased journal or printing required.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Observe: notice a detail. Question: something we want to find out. Represent: show an idea with a picture, gesture or words. Misconception: a guess is a detail we saw. Point to the actual drawing. If asked "Why does a leaf have lines?" Say that living leaves have veins that transport water and other materials; our drawing is a model, not a live leaf.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Invite wonder and a short original prayer if customary. Say C-STREAM is a time to notice, make, test and care; acronym recall is not the target.
    2. 4-8: Model "I see a line" versus "I wonder what the line does." Point to the evidence. Draw the detail, not a perfect leaf.
    3. 8-17: Partners inspect, swap pointing roles and each draw/select a detail. Ask "What can you point to?" Begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child points to a genuine detail and asks/selects one question. Offer "What does this part do?" or "Are all leaves alike?" Record support.
    5. 21-25: Two children share; retain dated sheets; count drawings and crayons; clear tables. Thank partners for listening.

    Success, access and SAFETY¶

    Success: each child connects a picture/gesture to an actual detail and a question. Do not score enthusiasm, letters or drawing realism. Support: offer two details; scribe an oral question. Challenge: ask how a question could be checked. Large pictures only for mouthing/allergy concerns; no taste, close smelling or collecting. Fully indoors.

    If things go wrong and family copy¶

    No leaf/drawing: draw a plain leaf with three branching lines on the board. Child only guesses: ask where the claimed feature appears; keep the question. Early finish: compare a partner's representation. Follow the routines' cleanup. Family: We noticed a detail and asked a question. Ask, "What did you actually see, and what do you still wonder?" No routine homework or supplies required.

    kindergartenroboticsalgorithms

    Weeks 2-3: Exploring Movement with Sphero¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / title K / Movement and instructions / Exploring Movement with Sphero
    Time Two meetings, each 25 minutes, including cleanup
    Meaningful domains C, T, M
    Big idea A tool responds to input; an algorithm is an ordered set of steps.
    Student objective "I can predict a two-step path, try it, and fix one step."
    Why Clear directions and checking results help us use tools responsibly.
    Catholic connection Include every partner in making decisions; tools should benefit people, not exclude them. CCC 2405, teacher paraphrase.
    Local standards CST-C2, CST-T1, CST-T2, CST-M1; local program codes, never official benchmarks. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology requirement Optional: picture-grid pathway is primary; real Sphero driving extends tool input/output.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Beginner / Light: 10 minutes for paper kits; optional robot setup 20 minutes plus charging / 3 minutes inside each meeting

    Before class¶

    1. Make 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 students: pairs, with a final trio for odd enrollment. Prepare ⅝/10/13 kits; the extra kit at 15/25 is a reserve. Assign chooser, mover, and checker; swap roles after each trial.
    2. Draw one 3-by-3 grid per pair, with 10 cm squares. Mark the lower-left square START and the upper-left square FINISH. Draw another target one square right of START. No printing is necessary.
    3. Make four large cards per pair: two upward arrows, one right arrow, one STOP hand. Here arrows mean one square up the page/right on the page, not a robot's facing direction.
    4. Draw a paper robot at least 8 cm wide per pair. Place kits at seated tables and write a roster with columns A (algorithm), I (input/output), H (real hardware drive), P (real programming).
    5. Optional hardware: use one school-approved, charged Sphero and one paired tablet. Before children arrive, open the installed Sphero Edu version, select the robot, enter Drive, aim/calibrate toward the far end, and test its lowest practical speed and stop control. Keep a 1 m clear demonstration lane and an adult beside it. If pairing or safe stopping fails, omit hardware. A substitute need not troubleshoot Bluetooth during class.

    Supplies and exact quantities¶

    Supply / allocation 10 15 20 25
    Per student: half-sheet observation paper; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Per pair/team: grid; large paper robot 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Per pair/team: four command cards 20 32 40 52
    Class: large demonstration grid and robot 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each
    Teacher: roster, timer 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each

    Optional class supplies, any enrollment: one robot, one tablet, one roll painter's tape. There is no class-set purchase or family donation requirement. Reuse grids/cards in meeting 2.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    • Input: what we give a tool; point to an arrow or control.
    • Output: what the tool does; move the paper robot.
    • Algorithm: steps in order; point left to right along cards.
    • Debug: find a mismatch, change a step, try again.

    A paper model follows the stated grid rule because a person moves it. In Drive mode an adult steers continuously; this is operating hardware, not writing a program. Real robots can drift, lose connection, or respond to sensors; they do not necessarily execute a command exactly.

    Misconception: "Robots know what I want." Explain that our model needs explicit steps; a machine depends on controls, software, sensors, and conditions.

    If asked, "Can robots think?" "Some machines use complicated software to choose actions. This classroom robot responds to its controls. It is not a person."

    SAFETY¶

    Keep children seated outside the optional robot lane. No chasing, racing, throwing, body maze, beanbag toss, or robot on a table edge. Stop the robot before retrieving it. Adult handles charging and battery compartments; inspect for damage. Use large paper pieces, not coins or tiny tokens. Offer seated pointing instead of body movement. Never physically guide a child's hands without permission.

    Meeting 1: input and output (25 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3 (3 min): Invite a brief prayer for including others. Show two arrow choices: "Which way will our robot move?"
    2. 3-7 (4 min): Model one arrow, one-square output, and STOP. Optional adult Drive demonstration replaces the last two minutes, not adds time. Name the difference between a card model and a real steering control.
    3. 7-16 (9 min): Pairs try UP then STOP and RIGHT then STOP from the same START. Swap roles every trial. Each child chooses and predicts one move before a partner executes it. Teacher begins individual I checks while circulating.
    4. 16-20 (4 min): Finish remaining I checks: child points to input and predicted/observed output. Accept pointing, speech, or drawing; do not repeat already documented checks.
    5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "What did we give it? What did it do? How did we include our partner?"
    6. 22-25 (3 min): Collect cards, park paper robots, return crayons; adult stops and stores optional hardware.

    Meeting 2: sequence and debugging (25 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3 (3 min): Recall input/output; show START and FINISH two squares up.
    2. 3-6 (3 min): Model UP, RIGHT: it misses FINISH. Ask "Which step needs changing?" Change RIGHT to UP; reset and retest.
    3. 6-15 (9 min): Pairs build UP, UP, STOP. Mover follows cards only. Each child then tries the intentionally wrong UP, RIGHT path and changes one card. Third child receives a full chooser turn, not just checker duty. Teacher starts individual A/count checks now.
    4. 15-20 (5 min): Finish remaining individual checks while partners rehearse: each child orders two arrows, predicts the endpoint, and corrects one wrong card. Record A and count two moves aloud/on fingers; no 25-child serial exit line.
    5. 20-22 (2 min): Share one correction and one fair-turn action.
    6. 22-25 (3 min): Reassemble four-card kits, collect grids and individual drawings, clear tables.

    Evidence and what success looks like¶

    Record I and A separately as independent / prompted / not yet. Success is a correct prediction of two one-square moves and a correction that reaches the pictured target, plus identifying a tool input/output. Neat writing, knowing left/right on one's body, or driving speed are not assessed.

    H may be recorded only for a child who actually controls the real robot and stops it safely; an adult demonstration is observation, not child operation. P stays not assessed in this unit. No-device success demonstrates algorithms and model input/output, not operating or programming real hardware.

    Questions, support, and troubleshooting¶

    • "What happens if we change the order? Did the output match your prediction?"
    • Support: offer two pictured choices; cover unused squares; child points while adult moves the token. Avoid screen or motor demands.
    • Challenge: design a three-command route and explain one correction; no speed competition.
    • Wrong route: reset to the same START, read one card at a time, and fix only the first mismatch.
    • Confused arrows: hold the page in one fixed orientation and point to the destination square.
    • Robot drift/disconnection: adult stops, checks aim once, then returns to paper; do not report a paper success as hardware success.
    • Minnesota indoor fallback: the seated grid is the full lesson in any weather. No outdoor or internet requirement.

    Optional family snippet¶

    We predicted and corrected picture instructions and practiced fair turns. Ask: "Show me two steps and one way to fix them." Real robot driving was optional and was recorded separately from algorithm learning. No homework or device purchase.

    kindergartenobservationstewardship

    Week 4: Wonder Walk¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / title K / Observation / Wonder Walk
    Time 25 minutes, including transitions and cleanup
    Domains / big idea C, S, A / Observations tell what we notice; questions tell what we want to find out.
    Student objective / why "I can show two details I noticed and ask one question." Careful looking helps us study and care for creation.
    Catholic connection Leave living things undisturbed and reuse materials; stewardship is a responsibility, not permission to take everything. CCC 2402, paraphrase.
    Local standards CST-C3, CST-S1, CST-A1; local, not official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty None / Beginner
    Prep / cleanup Light: 10 minutes / 3 minutes within lesson

    Before class¶

    1. Default indoor plan: seat pairs at tables. Provide one clean fallen leaf and one smooth rock at least 5 cm across per pair. Use large teacher-drawn leaf/rock pictures if allergies, mouthing, or availability make specimens unsuitable. Say that a drawing is a representation, not a specimen.
    2. Fold a half-sheet into two observation boxes for each child; put crayons within reach. Draw an eye and a question mark on the board.
    3. With 10/15/20/25 students, make 5/7/10/12 teams (pairs/final trio) and prepare ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment. A third child receives their own paper and a turn with each object.
    4. Optional outdoor path: school policy permits it only with required adult coverage, accessible dry route, safe weather, and no icy surfaces. Choose two stops within a two-minute walk. If clothing/transit would exceed the four-minute allowance, use indoors. Check headcount at exit, each stop, and return; do not assume 25 children can be supervised outdoors by one adult.

    Materials¶

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Per student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Per team: large leaf/picture; large rock/picture; tray 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Optional per team: magnifier 5 8 10 13
    Teacher/class: eye/question drawings; roster; timer 1 set 1 set 1 set 1 set

    Outdoor only: one rigid paper backing per child (10/15/20/25); no collection bags or camera needed. Teacher checks specimens and supplies handwashing access.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Observe: notice with safe senses; point to eyes. Detail: a small part you notice, such as a vein or speckle. Question: something to investigate. Stewardship: careful use and care.

    A detached leaf was part of a living plant; a rock was not. Do not classify living things by movement alone or demand a living/nonliving judgment about a detached leaf. Plants are alive although they do not walk. Observation can include accessible hearing, touch of approved items, or description; sight is not the only valid pathway.

    Misconception: "My guess is something I saw." Distinguish "I see lines" from "I think water goes through them."

    If asked, "Why does a leaf have lines?" "The lines include veins that carry water and other materials. We can see a pattern; our drawing alone does not prove what is inside."

    SAFETY¶

    No tasting, unknown plants, wild mushrooms, animal remains, feathers, nest disturbance, or smelling unknown materials closely. Adults inspect/clean specimens; pictures are equivalent observation targets when needed. No looking at the Sun through eyes or magnifiers. Keep magnifiers out of direct sun; wash hands after specimens. No collection or picking. Cancel outdoor work for cold, ice, storms, unsafe heat, or insufficient staffing.

    Numbered sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-3 (3 min): Brief prayer for care of creation. Model "I notice a line" and "I wonder where it goes." Explain safe looking and gentle hands.
    2. 3-5 (2 min): Indoors: distribute trays and demonstrate passing. Outdoors: walk to first stop and count children.
    3. 5-11 (6 min): Look at first object/stop. Each child points to one detail, then draws it in box 1 or dictates while adult sketches. Ask "What do you actually notice?"
    4. 11-17 (6 min): Pass second object/observe second stop without moving away from the group. Add a second detail in box 2. Partner asks one question using "I wonder..." or chooses between teacher's two question pictures. Teacher begins recording individual detail/question evidence now.
    5. 17-19 (2 min): Indoors: return trays. Outdoors: return inside and count children. Keep drawings.
    6. 19-22 (3 min): Finish remaining individual checks during paired sharing: each child shows two details and a question. Do not repeat documented checks or require 25 serial speeches. Ask "How did we care for the things we studied?"
    7. 22-25 (3 min): Collect reusable materials, wash hands, save drawings. Teacher adds one question to the Wonder Wall later, not extra class time.

    Evidence and success¶

    On the roster record two observed details and one question for every child: independent / prompted / not yet. A child may point, dictate, sketch, or choose a picture; do not judge realistic drawing skill. Successful evidence is specific ("three lines," "bumpy edge"), not just "I liked it." One stewardship action is returning materials or leaving an organism untouched.

    Questions and contingencies¶

    • "Which detail can you show me? Which idea would we need to test?"
    • Support: use large drawings, tactile approved leaf models, oral description, two pictured choices, or a seated observation partner.
    • Challenge: compare the two objects using a visible feature and ask a testable question.
    • No specimens/magnifiers: use large teacher drawings and naked-eye observation; report observations of the drawings honestly.
    • Too many questions: collect one per child orally; the adult may jot a key word rather than a full sentence.
    • Minnesota indoor fallback: use the default table lesson unchanged at -10 F. A nearby window is optional, not a required outdoor view.

    Optional family snippet¶

    We drew or described two observed details, asked a question, and practiced leaving creation undisturbed. Ask: "What did you notice, and what do you still wonder?" A safe window observation is optional; nothing must be brought from home.

    Weeks 5-6: Building with KEVA Planks¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Structures / two meetings of 25 minutes each
    Domains / big idea C, E, M; the base and arrangement affect whether a structure stays standing
    Student objective / why "I can count blocks, test a low tower, change its base and test again." Evidence helps builders improve.
    Catholic connection Care for shared tools and others' work; skilled work can serve people.
    Local standards CST-C3: resource care; CST-E2: before/after test; CST-M1: count up to ten chosen blocks. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 10 minutes / 4 minutes in each meeting

    Before class and exact materials¶

    Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams and ⅝/10/13 budgeted kits. Inspect blocks; test one low six-block model; draw a two-attempt picture record. KEVA is optional branding; ordinary large stable wooden blocks work.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: 20 large blocks 100 160 200 260
    Kit: tray/mat 5 8 10 13
    Student: sheet; crayon, per meeting 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer, roster and one shared measuring ruler. Demonstrate using a budgeted kit, then return it. Retain the first meeting's sheets at school.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Base: bottom supporting parts. Stable: stands without a hand holding it. Test: check against a criterion. Redesign: change and test again. Misconception: tallest means best. Criterion is ten seconds unaided, with the same six blocks, not maximum height. If asked why a tower falls: identify slipping, leaning or a changed support; do not promise widening always wins.

    Meeting 1: a fair starting test, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Discuss buildings serving people and caring for shared supplies.
    2. 4-8: Model six blocks on a low base. Teacher times ten seconds, hands away.
    3. 8-17: Partners build with six selected blocks, swap turns, count and test. Teacher gives a common start/stop signal; begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child counts the chosen set, points to the base and reports standing/falling. Record actual results, including falls.
    5. 21-25: Draw/retain a first-attempt picture; count blocks back; clear trays.

    Meeting 2: change and retest, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve drawings, not unverifiable memories. Restate six blocks/ten seconds.
    2. 4-8: Demonstrate changing only base arrangement with the same blocks.
    3. 8-17: Each partner chooses a base change, rebuilds and observes the same timed test. Rotate the trio's builder turn; start individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Child indicates the change, counts the set and compares two outcomes. Ask "What stayed the same? Did your change help in this test?"
    5. 21-25: Save dated evidence, return all 20 kit blocks, thank partners, clear.

    Success, support, challenge and SAFETY¶

    Record counting, observed result and tested change separately. Falling is evidence, not failure of a child. Support: a three-block model and prompted count, with reduced criterion recorded. Challenge: repeat the six-block test to check reliability, not height. Build seated below shoulder height; no throwing, walking gallery, shaking another model or standing on furniture.

    Troubleshooting, indoor alternative and family copy¶

    Missing first sheet: run a fresh first test, label it today, then compare. No blocks: groups <=3 may share kits using the routines; do not claim a paper picture is a tested tower. Repeated collapse: use flat blocks on a wider base. All work indoors. Family: We counted blocks and compared a ten-second test before and after a change. Ask, "What changed, and what did the test show?"

    Weeks 7-9: Engineering Helpers¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Service design / three 25-minute meetings
    Domains / big idea C, E, A, M; a useful design must meet a user's stated need and a test
    Student objective / why "I can plan a tray, carry two empty cups, change a part and retest." Engineers use evidence to serve people.
    Catholic connection Listen to a requested need; respect people rather than assuming incapacity.
    Local standards CST-C2: need/inclusion; CST-E1: carrying criterion; CST-E2: test/redesign; CST-A1: plan; CST-M1: count two cups. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first kit, 5 reset / 4 per meeting

    Before class and exact materials¶

    Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits. On each desk mark a 30 cm path. Tell this complete fictional request: "Our classroom helper asks for a tray to move two empty cups from one mark to the other without either falling." Precut smooth cardboard and tape; pretest a flat tray at slow walking-hand speed.

    Kit/student allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: two cups; two 20 cm cardboard squares 10 each 16 each 20 each 26 each
    Kit: ten craft sticks; ten 10 cm tape strips 50 each 80 each 100 each 130 each
    Kit: storage tray 5 8 10 13
    Student: plan/evidence sheet; crayon, per meeting 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: ruler, timer, roster, pencil; adult-only scissors. Demonstrate with a budgeted kit. Store work by kit number; no family materials or purchased unit.

    Vocabulary, background and SAFETY¶

    Need: a requested problem. Criterion: what the model must do. Plan: drawing before making. Redesign: a change informed by a test. A rim may retain cups but can use extra material; test rather than promise. Misconception: decoration proves a helper works. Ask about the same two cups and path. If asked about helping a real person, say this is a desk model only. No liquid, loaded glasses, high shelves, climbing, wearables, pets, infants, disability simulation or trial of an actual assistive device.

    Meeting 1: ask, plan and try, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Read the fictional request; each child names who asks and what they need.
    2. 4-8: Demonstrate two cups/path; draw a flat-tray plan and the pass condition.
    3. 8-17: Children draw a plan, count two cups and try moving them on a flat piece. Swap chooser/mover/checker roles; begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Child points to their plan and explains/indicates the criterion, not just appearance. Record whether both cups remained aboard.
    5. 21-25: Date drawings; store dry labeled kits; count and clear.

    Meeting 2: make and collect a first result, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve plans and re-read the request.
    2. 4-8: Model folding a low edge and attaching it with precut tape.
    3. 8-17: Build from the two cardboard pieces, at most ten sticks and ten strips. Each child handles an appropriate construction step and observes a slow test.
    4. 17-21: Record cups aboard, 0/½, and where a cup moved. Child shows a result on the plan; drawing/pointing is sufficient.
    5. 21-25: Retain the first-result sheets and dry models; reset trays.

    Meeting 3: evidence-led redesign, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve results. A missing result is collected freshly, not invented.
    2. 4-8: Model changing one edge, keeping the same cups/path and slow movement.
    3. 8-17: Partners propose one change, retest and swap roles. Count cups remaining and begin each child's evidence check.
    4. 17-21: Each child points to a changed part, compares two results and explains whether it met the requested need. Keep unsuccessful results too.
    5. 21-25: Save evidence, remove reusable sticks, sort dry scraps and clear.

    Success, questions, troubleshooting and access¶

    Check requested need, plan, two-cup count and tested change separately. Ask "What stayed the same? Which part changed first? Who requested this?" Support: adult-started folds, two choices, dictated explanation. Challenge: explain a material tradeoff without claiming real-device safety. Insufficient cardboard: fold stiff school cardstock to the same size and record the material used. No stored model: rebuild a simple first version and take a fresh result. All work is indoors; never turn a missing kit into an unsafe real-person challenge.

    Family: We planned a desk model, moved two empty cups and retested one change. Ask, "What did your test show?" Models are not real assistive devices; no homework, donation or home testing.

    Week 10: Bridges Connect Us¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Structures / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea C, E, M; a deck crosses a gap and supports hold it up
    Student objective / why "I can show supports, test a deck, change it and retest." Bridges provide access; models help us reason safely.
    Catholic connection Name someone a safe crossing could serve; inclusion is not a structural test.
    Local standards CST-C2: access need; CST-E1: gap/load criterion; CST-E2: retest; CST-M1: count supports/load. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and quantities¶

    Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits. Place two equal-height large blocks 5 cm apart on each tray, with one 20-by-10 cm cardboard deck. Pretest one identical large wooden block as load; no tiny cars/coins required. The criterion is spanning the gap and holding this load for three seconds.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: two supports + one load block 15 24 30 39
    Kit: two cardboard deck pieces 10 16 20 26
    Kit: tray; ruler 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer/roster, demonstration from one kit. No school-owned specialty set assumed.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Support: holds up a deck. Deck: crossing surface. Gap: open space. Retest: repeat the same check after a change. Folding can change stiffness. Misconception: any short plank spans any gap. Use the supplied long deck, not a six-inch gap with a short plank. If asked about a real bridge, explain that our model cannot establish safety for people.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Draw two places across a stream; ask who needs access. State criterion.
    2. 4-8: Show supports/deck, count two supports and one load; place the load gently at the deck's center for three timed seconds, then remove it.
    3. 8-17: Partners test version 1, fold the second deck into a shallow channel and retest. Keep support gap, load and location the same. Swap roles; begin individual checks and record a fall honestly.
    4. 17-21: Each child indicates support/deck, counts the parts, and reports before/after results and a changed feature. Ask "What stayed the same?"
    5. 21-25: Save dated sketches, return/count blocks and rulers, flatten reusable cardboard, clear trays. No walking or sequential whole-class load queue.

    Success, SAFETY, support and troubleshooting¶

    Success is identifying parts/criterion and comparing two actual tests, not a pretty or successful bridge alone. Desk models only; no person/pet weight, throwing, tall supports or fingers under the load. Adult-inspected smooth blocks. Support: prestarted folds, adult placement directed by the child. Challenge: repeat to check whether the result agrees. Missing blocks: two equal-height closed books and one identical large classroom load per kit, pretested by the teacher; record the substitute material. No safe load: defer load evidence, teach parts only and report the change. Fully indoors in any weather.

    Family: We counted supports and compared two same-load bridge tests. Ask, "What changed and what stayed the same?" No homework or model use by people.

    Week 11: Coding Thankfulness¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Algorithms / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea C, T, A; ordered instructions can deliver a respectful message
    Objective / why "I can predict two moves and fix a wrong step." Clear instructions help us communicate.
    Catholic connection Gratitude and care for a recipient; no forced family disclosure or presumed need.
    Local standards CST-C2: respectful recipient; CST-T2: prediction/correction; CST-A3: message. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional ScratchJr extension, paper primary / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and materials¶

    Read K routines. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits for 10/15/20/25 pupils; active teams 5/7/10/12. Draw a 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left and recipient one square right and one up. Draw four large cards: RIGHT, UP, DOWN, STOP. Arrows refer to the page. Use an 8 cm paper token with a child's drawn gratitude image.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: grid; token 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Kit: four large cards 20 32 40 52
    Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer/roster; model with one budgeted kit. No word cards, projector or account.

    Vocabulary, background and SAFETY¶

    Algorithm: steps in order. Predict: say where steps will end. Debug: find and correct an error. Message: idea for another person. Misconception: a motion-lines drawing is executable code. A person follows our paper rules; that is an algorithm model, not software execution. If asked about computers, explain that real programs must be run on a device. Desk grids, large parts, no body maze, small tokens or public student uploads.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Choose a school helper or trusted recipient; draw/describe a thankful message without sharing private details. Original prayer optional.
    2. 4-8: Model RIGHT, DOWN, STOP missing the target. Reset; replace DOWN with UP and test again. STOP is not a movement.
    3. 8-17: Partners predict RIGHT, UP, STOP, follow cards, reset and fix the intentionally wrong path. Rotate each planner/mover turn; begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child predicts the endpoint, changes one wrong card and explains/points to the message's meaning and recipient.
    5. 21-25: Share two messages without personal information; store four-card kits, retain dated records and clear.

    Success, support, troubleshooting and extension¶

    Record prediction, tested correction and communicated meaning separately. Ask "Which step changed? Did the output match?" Support: two pictured choices and adult movement directed by the child. Challenge: test reversed order. Misoriented grid: fix page orientation before retesting. Missing cards: draw arrows on ordinary paper. Entire primary lesson works indoors without devices.

    Optional digital extension: only after regular-teacher compatibility/ access preflight, replace practice time with an already-open ScratchJr project. Attach a green-flag start followed by two blue movement blocks; tap the flag, observe, change a direction and rerun. Each child must execute to receive software evidence; observing or paper movement does not qualify. Installed controls: ScratchJr interface. If setup fails, return to paper and mark execution unassessed.

    Family: We communicated thanks and corrected picture instructions. Ask, "Which card did you change?" No home app, purchase or routine homework.

    Week 12: Making Gifts for Others¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Service art / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea C, A; visual choices help a recipient understand a message
    Objective / why "I can choose a picture for someone, explain it and make it clearer." Art communicates care.
    Catholic connection Respect the recipient's wishes; gifts are not proof that a person needs rescuing.
    Local standards CST-C2: dignity/recipient; CST-A2: purposeful choice; CST-A3: explanation/revision. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 10 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and supplies¶

    Read K routines. Teacher offers a card for a school helper or child-chosen trusted person. Arrange school-approved delivery first; if acceptance is unknown retain it as a communication model. Precut four paper shapes at least 5 cm per child. Fold one sheet into a card; a second sheet is the plan.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Student: two sheets 20 30 40 50
    Student: four large shapes 40 60 80 100
    Student: crayon 10 15 20 25
    Kit: glue stick, pairs/final trio plus reserve 5 8 10 13

    Teacher: timer/roster, adult scissors, one sample made from budgeted materials.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Recipient: person the message is for. Plan: picture of the idea. Choice: feature selected for a reason. Revise: make meaning clearer. Misconception: more decorations make the best gift. Judge communicated meaning, not polish or expense. If asked whether this is engineering, say today's target is art/service; no functional engineering test is claimed.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Discuss caring without assuming every recipient likes the same gift. Ask "Who is it for, and what message will it carry?"
    2. 4-8: Show a simple unclear drawing, add one meaningful feature and explain why. Model a plan with no required words.
    3. 8-17: Each child plans and makes a card; partners point to the main idea and give one respectful suggestion. Revise a feature; begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child identifies recipient and a purposeful shape/color/ picture choice, then indicates a change making the message clearer.
    5. 21-25: Retain evidence/arrange approved delivery, count shapes, cap glue, collect crayons and clear.

    Success, SAFETY, access and troubleshooting¶

    Record recipient awareness, choice/reason and communication revision. Do not grade handwriting, expense, artistic realism or personal piety. Support: large ready-folded card, two picture choices, adult scribing. Challenge: explain how spacing/contrast helps the recipient. No sequins, glitter, ribbon, food, unsafe tiny stickers or public names/images. No recipient permission: keep the card in class; no external visit. No glue: draw shapes directly and assess the same design choices. All work indoors; no family donation or required home delivery.

    Family: We made and revised a thoughtful visual message. Ask, "Why did you choose that picture, and what did you change?" No routine homework.

    Week 13: Fall Celebration¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Evidence reflection / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea C, A; an enjoyable memory and a demonstrated skill are different
    Objective / why "I can show evidence of one discovery and explain it." Honest reflection helps us choose what to practice.
    Catholic connection Thank others and report what we actually demonstrated; do not exaggerate.
    Local standards CST-C1: honest claim/evidence; CST-A3: communicate/revise. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved documentation camera; no device needed / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and materials¶

    Read K routines. Retrieve one dated work sheet per child if available. Otherwise use the fresh paper test below; never invent an earlier result. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits with a 3-by-3 grid, large paper token and RIGHT/UP/STOP cards.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: grid; token 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Kit: three cards 15 24 30 39
    Student: evidence half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: roster/timer and demonstration from one kit. No treats, certificates, photo collection or slideshow required. Optional camera use follows school consent.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Evidence: work/result supporting a claim. Demonstrate: show a skill. Favorite: something enjoyed. Practice: work on a skill not yet secure. Misconception: attending means mastery. A partner's result does not prove this child's understanding. If asked about a missing portfolio, collect a new dated demonstration and label it today, not as a past event.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Celebrate effort; contrast "I liked robots" with "I predicted this path."
    2. 4-8: Model explaining a dated result. For fresh evidence demonstrate RIGHT, UP, STOP from the lower-left square and reset.
    3. 8-17: Each child chooses existing evidence and rehearses its explanation, or predicts/follows the fresh route. Swap turns; begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Child shows one actual result, explains it and changes a drawing/ gesture if the listener cannot understand. Record any prompted evidence.
    5. 21-25: Neighboring partners share concurrently; retain dated sheets, return cards/crayons and clear. No 25-child presentation queue.

    Success, access, SAFETY and troubleshooting¶

    Check claim matches actual evidence and communicates a meaning. Favorite activity, certificate and attractive drawing are not skill evidence. Support: two sample explanations and pointing. Challenge: name a limit or next practice step. Desk-only large paper pieces; no snack/allergy or body-maze activity. Child cannot recall: use the fresh route, not a leading invented memory. No prior work: the supplied paper test is the complete indoor pathway. Optional camera documents evidence but does not substitute for observing it.

    Family: We celebrated an actual discovery and named something to practice. Ask, "What can you show me, and what does it show?" Home work is optional.

    Weeks 14-15: Light All Around¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Light and design / two 25-minute meetings
    Domains / big idea C, S, T, A; materials transmit light differently and artists choose materials for a purpose
    Objective / why "I can compare three materials and explain a tissue placement choice." Fair tests inform design.
    Catholic connection Report actual results; a classroom light symbol is not scientific proof of a belief.
    Local standards CST-C1: evidence/symbol distinction; CST-S2: comparison; CST-T1: flashlight input/output; CST-A2: design choice. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None for digital devices / guided / 15 minutes first kit / 4 per meeting

    Before class and exact materials¶

    Read K routines. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, 5/7/10/12 active teams. Inspect secured flashlight battery covers; teacher alone handles cells. Precut a 10 cm rigid clear plastic square with smooth edges, tissue square and cardboard square per kit. Mark lamp/material/white-screen positions at 10 cm intervals. Pretest at normal room lighting; adjust screen position for visible results, then keep it fixed.

    Allocation for both meetings 10 15 20 25
    Kit: flashlight; each of 3 test squares; white screen 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Student: large precut paper frame; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Student: two tissue art squares 20 30 40 50
    Student: four 5 cm tape strips 40 60 80 100

    Teacher: timer/roster, scissors for advance preparation, demonstration from one kit. Total tissue test/art squares: 25/38/50/63. Keep first results at school.

    Vocabulary, background and SAFETY¶

    Source: makes light. Transmit: lets light through. Opaque: blocks transmission in this test. Symbol: represents a meaning, not a measured fact. Clear plastic transmits much light; tissue scatters/transmits some; cardboard usually blocks it. Describe actual outcomes, not guaranteed brightness. Misconception: tissue is fully transparent. If asked whether paper makes light, explain it reflects/transmits source light; it is not itself a light source. No Sun viewing, beams at eyes, flames, lasers, glass, tubes, loose wrap, accessible batteries or student circuit building. Keep the room safely lit.

    Meeting 1: material comparison, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Identify lamp as source; distinguish a taught faith symbol from an observation.
    2. 4-8: Model flashlight switch input/output and one material at fixed marked distances. Look at the screen, not into the beam.
    3. 8-17: Partners predict and compare all three squares, holding lamp, screen and material positions constant. Swap roles; begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child classifies one actual outcome as clear/fuzzy/blocked and identifies a kept-same condition and flashlight control.
    5. 21-25: Date results, switch off lamps, return three squares and clear.

    Meeting 2: evidence-informed art, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve results; if absent run a fresh tissue/cardboard comparison.
    2. 4-8: Model tissue placement in a precut frame; choose a position to make a pattern readable. No required holiday date or devotional history.
    3. 8-17: Each child chooses and tapes tissue placement, compares its light effect at the marked position and revises one choice after peer feedback.
    4. 17-21: Child explains/points to the purposeful choice and distinguishes what the test showed from a classroom meaning of the symbol.
    5. 21-25: Retain evidence, switch off/count lights, collect dry scraps and clear.

    Success, access, troubleshooting and reported holdings¶

    Assess prediction/result, kept-same condition, input/output and artistic reason separately; color beauty is not mastery. Support: two material choices, adult placement directed by child, tactile shapes. Challenge: compare repeat tests. No visible result: teacher adjusts screen before issuing kits; record adjustments. No secured lights: use inspected source/class demonstration and record student operation unassessed; never improvise a battery circuit. All work indoors.

    Reported OLP holding, preserved: 8 Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135. Count, completeness, location, manufacturer age/power guidance and condition remain unverified. See reported holdings. Only a pretested adult-operated demonstration is optional; the flashlight minimum is unchanged, no loan or student circuit objective is added.

    Family: We compared light through materials and made a purposeful art choice. Ask, "What did you observe, and what did your picture mean?" No homework.

    Week 16: Star of Wonder¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Stars and models / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea S, A, M; a drawn pattern represents stars but does not make light or show actual distances
    Objective / why "I can count five star dots and explain that my picture is a model." Models help communicate ideas while leaving things out.
    Catholic connection Wonder at creation and truthful explanation; no physical cause for the biblical star is claimed.
    Local standards CST-S3: model/limit; CST-A1: representation; CST-M1: count 3-5 dots. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and materials¶

    Read K routines. Draw five separated dots, numbered for the teacher only, in a simple zigzag on one kit card. It is an invented pattern, not an official constellation. Budget ⅝/10/13 cards for active 5/7/10/12 pair/trio teams.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: five-dot model card 5 8 10 13
    Student: sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer/roster, demonstration from one card. No stickers, glitter, glue, night visit, Sun viewing or device required.

    Vocabulary, background and source¶

    Star: makes its own light. Pattern: arrangement we recognize. Model: representation with limits. The Sun is a star; stars remain present in daytime even when difficult to see. Our dots are not stars at equal real distances; a crayon does not produce light. Source inspected October 4: NASA stars, teacher paraphrase. Misconception: stars physically have five points. Say pointed paper shapes are symbols; real stars are not paper cutouts. If asked about Magi, use only the school's approved religion material; number, travel time and astronomical explanation are not needed or asserted here.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Invite wonder; compare a real light-producing star with a picture.
    2. 4-8: Model one-to-one counting of five dots and drawing their arrangement. Explain the picture does not show actual size/distance.
    3. 8-17: Partners point/count and each make a model with 3-5 dots. Swap roles; child chooses spacing to help a partner recognize it. Begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child counts their dots and explains/points to a model limit: not actual stars, not producing light, or not real distances.
    5. 21-25: Neighbor partners interpret the pictures; retain dated work, return cards/crayons and clear.

    Success, questions, SAFETY and troubleshooting¶

    Check count matches dots, recognizable representation and one limit separately. Ask "What is real in the sky? What can this picture not tell us?" Support: three large dots, tactile raised paper marks/adult scribing. Challenge: same five dots drawn differently, explaining that lines are our drawing choice. No Sun/night observations or dark room. Child draws pointed stars: accept the symbol, then explicitly distinguish shape from the real object. No dark paper: ordinary paper works; no supply purchase is necessary.

    Family: We counted a star-pattern model and explained what it cannot show. Ask, "Does your picture make light like a star?" No required evening outing.

    Week 18: New Year Goals¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Observation and practice goals / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea C, S, M, A; a goal needs an action and evidence, not a wish or promise
    Objective / why "I can record what I observe in the sky and choose a way to check it again." Repeated records help us compare conditions.
    Catholic connection Honest observations and patient practice, not a claim that God guarantees a particular result.
    Local standards CST-C1: truthful record; CST-S1: observation; CST-S3: weather representation; CST-M2: symbol record; CST-A3: communicate goal. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 5 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and supplies¶

    Read K routines. From a safe indoor window away from the Sun, identify sky as mostly clear, partly cloudy or mostly cloud covered. Draw three large cloud-coverage symbols per kit. Make no temperature/wind inference from appearance. If pupils cannot view the sky, teacher supplies a dated first-hand description and labels it teacher observation, not the child's measurement.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: three large symbols 15 24 30 39
    Student: dated record sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12. Teacher: timer, roster, class record sheet with date and observation time. Store it for Week 20, not at home.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Observation: what was seen/described now. Record: saved information. Goal: skill to practice. Prediction: expected future result, not today's observation. One record cannot establish a seasonal pattern or forecast. Misconception: a drawing of a sunny sky means it is warm. Explain we have not measured outdoor temperature. If asked about tomorrow, label any answer a guess.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Reframe goals as checkable practice. Ask "How could we show learning?"
    2. 4-8: Model selecting today's sky symbol and dating the record; distinguish observation from a picture of preferred weather.
    3. 8-17: Observe safely or listen to the labeled teacher report; each child chooses/draws a matching symbol and describes the evidence. Begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Child explains today's record and chooses the goal "record the sky again and compare" with a pointing/drawing reminder. Do not award future mastery.
    5. 21-25: Save individual/class records for Week 20, collect symbols/crayons, clear. No compulsory between-class or home observation.

    Success, access, SAFETY and troubleshooting¶

    Check record matches actual report, child distinguishes now from a guess and states a checkable next action. Support: two symbol choices, read-aloud/tactile symbols and adult scribing. Challenge: identify what was not measured. No outdoor exposure, Sun viewing, climbing to windows or forced sensory task. No visible sky/teacher report: use an explicitly invented practice picture, mark model data and defer actual-weather evidence. Week 20 provides a fresh real record when possible; never invent the previous observation.

    Family: We practiced a weather record and a checkable goal. Ask, "What did you observe, and how will you check it again?" No homework.

    Weeks 19-22: Exploration Stations¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Practice and evidence / four meetings, each 25 minutes
    Domains / big idea S, T, E, A, M; practice means checking results, not collecting a station stamp
    Objective / why "I can retest, compare records, explain a pattern and fix instructions." Transfer makes skills usable.
    Catholic connection Fair turns and honest reporting; no claim that everyone mastered every field.
    Local standards CST-S1: actual observation; CST-T2: correction; CST-E2: retest; CST-A2: purposeful readable pattern; CST-M2: weather/pattern representation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional pretested robot extension, paper primary / guided / 15 minutes per prepared kit / 4 each meeting

    Before class and exact supplies¶

    Read K routines. One challenge occupies the whole class per meeting; no five-station rotation or passport. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits for 5/7/10/12 active teams. Every meeting uses 10/15/20/25 student half-sheets/crayons plus one teacher timer/roster. Demonstrate with a budgeted kit; return it before practice.

    Meeting / kit allocation 10 15 20 25
    19: 20 large blocks; one tray 100 / 5 160 / 8 200 / 10 260 / 13
    20: three sky-symbol cards 15 24 30 39
    21: three circles and three squares, >=5 cm 15 each 24 each 30 each 39 each
    22: grid; >=8 cm token; four command cards 5 / 5 / 20 8 / 8 / 32 10 / 10 / 40 13 / 13 / 52

    For 20 retrieve Week 18's dated sky record if it is a real observation. If missing, prepare to record at this meeting's beginning and again at minute 17; label both date/time. Do not invent yesterday's weather. For 22 draw a 3-by-3 grid with START lower-left; cards RIGHT, UP, DOWN, STOP.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Retest: repeat a check. Record: saved information. Repeat: recurring unit in a pattern. Debug: correct instructions. Misconception: visiting a station proves mastery. Each child supplies the specific evidence below. If asked why weather did not change, explain that unchanged observations are valid; two records cannot establish a season. Pattern drawings are representations; paper routes are not software/hardware operation.

    Meeting 19: structure retest, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Recall a low six-block tower's ten-second unaided criterion.
    2. 4-8: Model a base change with the same six blocks and timing.
    3. 8-17: Partners test, change base and retest; swap roles and begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child indicates a change and compares two actual results, including a fall. Save a two-result drawing.
    5. 21-25: Count blocks, retain dated evidence, clear trays.

    Meeting 20: two weather records, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Safely observe sky/cloud coverage away from the Sun; date/time a first record if no actual previous class record exists.
    2. 4-8: Model mostly clear/partly cloudy/mostly covered symbols. Explain that a forecast, preferred picture or room temperature is not this observation.
    3. 8-17: Children select/draw today's symbol and compare a prior actual record when available. Identify matching/different features; begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Make a second timed observation if using the same-day route. Each child compares the two labeled records and states what was observed.
    5. 21-25: Save records with dates/times; collect cards/crayons and clear.

    Meeting 21: a readable repeat, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Name circle/square and a repeated unit, not a favorite color.
    2. 4-8: Model circle-square-circle-square and predict next circle-square.
    3. 8-17: Partners arrange/extend six pieces; swap turns and change spacing to make the pattern readable to a partner. Begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child selects the next two shapes and explains/points to why the spacing or arrangement helps communication.
    5. 21-25: Save a drawing, count three of each shape per kit, clear.

    Meeting 22: sequence correction, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Target is one square right and one up from START.
    2. 4-8: Model RIGHT, DOWN, STOP missing it; reset and correct DOWN to UP.
    3. 8-17: Every child predicts, follows and corrects the path in a full turn; partners move only by the shown rule. Begin checks.
    4. 17-21: Child shows endpoint and tested correction; save individual evidence.
    5. 21-25: Repack grids/tokens/cards, retain evidence and clear.

    Success, SAFETY, access and troubleshooting¶

    Record four separate checks across the unit, not one participation score. Support: a modeled choice, large tactile shapes, adult-directed movement or scribing. Challenge: fair repeated test, record limitation, new repeat or reversed route. No height contests, small tokens, body mazes, unknown nature items, Sun viewing or outdoor prerequisite; structures stay low and seated. No sky view: labeled teacher observation, or explicitly model data with actual-weather evidence deferred. Missing blocks: shared <=3 groups, same test. All minimum pathways are indoors and device-free.

    Optional robot extension is a separately pretested teacher choice; charge/aim and verify compatible controls before class. Replace, do not add, work time; actual operation/execution evidence requires each child's real device turn. If equipment fails, paper evidence remains computational thinking only.

    Family: We checked structure changes, two weather records, a readable repeat and picture instructions. Ask about one actual result, not a station stamp. No homework or donations.

    Week 23: Catholic Schools Week¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Truthful learning display / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea C, T, A; a display communicates actual evidence and protects private information
    Objective / why "I can show a result and help someone understand it." Clear explanations share learning with our community.
    Catholic connection Faith and reason support truthful inquiry; gratitude does not replace evidence.
    Local standards CST-C1: honest result; CST-T3: private-information/adult-help scenario; CST-A3: audience explanation/revision. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved photography; none needed / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

    Before class and quantities¶

    Read K routines. Use actual school event dates, not a presumed calendar week. Retrieve one dated test/observation sheet per child. Missing work has a fresh route: 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left, target right then up; RIGHT/UP/STOP cards. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: grid; large token; three cards 5 / 5 / 15 8 / 8 / 24 10 / 10 / 30 13 / 13 / 39
    Student: display/evidence sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Teacher: two hypothetical sharing cards 2 2 2 2

    Teacher: timer/roster, demonstration from a kit and an approved classroom display space. Visitors, public photography, outside contact and personal names are not required. Draw a house icon to represent a fictional person's home address, and an anonymous shape pattern. Read their meanings aloud; no actual address or student data is written or requested.

    Vocabulary, background and SAFETY¶

    Evidence: actual work/result. Audience: person interpreting the display. Explain: tell what a result means. Revise: make a message clearer. Misconception: a favorite photograph proves every skill. A child must identify what was actually demonstrated. If asked whether prayer proves a science claim, say our faith reflection and test result are different kinds of statement. If asked about sharing, a home address stays private; ask the trusted school adult before public sharing. An anonymous pattern is not personal information, but school permission still applies to publication. Seated desk models, large paper parts; no public names/images without approval.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Invite thanks for school/community and state the truthful-display goal.
    2. 4-8: Model a result plus explanation. If no work exists, run RIGHT, UP, STOP freshly; date it today and do not claim a robot ran. Read the two hypothetical sharing cards and model keeping the address private.
