    🤲 Weeks 26-27: Helping Hands Design¶

    Unit Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 2 sessions (30 min each)
    STREAM Focus E (Engineering), R (Religion), A (Art)

    Weeks 26-27: Helping Hands Design¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Apply human-centered design thinking 2. Create solutions that address real needs 3. Test and iterate on designs 4. Present design solutions

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Connect Catholic Social Teaching to design 2. Understand preferential option for the poor 3. Practice empathy and compassion in design thinking

    Weeks 26-27: Helping Hands Design¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details¶

    Catholic Social Teaching: Preferential Option for the Poor — God calls us to care especially for those who are struggling. Engineers and designers can create things that help people in need.

    Scripture reference¶

    Matthew 25:40; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies¶

    St. Vincent de Paul — He organized practical help for poor people. He found creative solutions to help those in need with food, medicine, and shelter.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • Design scenario cards

    • Planning worksheets

    • Building materials: cardboard, paper, tape, craft supplies

    • Testing materials

    • Presentation space

    Session 1: Design for Others¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer & Introduction (4 min)¶

    Prayer: "Jesus, You said when we help others, we help You. Open our hearts to see the needs of others. Guide our hands as we design to help. Amen."

    Read Matthew 25:40 only from the approved Bible; do not reproduce an unverified abbreviated quotation.

    Discuss: "Who are 'the least of these'? Who needs help?"

    Design Challenge Introduction (6 min)¶

    Present scenarios (choose one for class):

    Scenario A: "An elderly person has trouble carrying groceries."

    • What's hard for them?

    • What would help?

    Scenario B: "A child in a wheelchair can't reach drinking fountains."

    • What's the problem?

    • What could we design?

    Scenario C: "Someone who can't see needs help knowing what's around them."

    • What challenges do they face?

    • How could we help?

    Empathy discussion:

    • "How would YOU feel if you had this challenge?"

    • "What would you want someone to design for you?"

    Design Thinking: Brainstorm & Plan (15 min)¶

    Individual brainstorm (4 min): Draw 2-3 ideas.

    Partner share (4 min): Share ideas with partner. Combine ideas!

    Choose and plan (7 min):

    • Select one design to build

    • Draw detailed plan

    • List materials needed

    • Identify how you'll test if it works

    Closing Preview (5 min)¶

    Share plans with another group.

    Faith Connection: "When we design to help others, we're doing what Jesus asked! We're being His hands in the world."

    Closing Prayer: "Bless our designs, Lord. Help us think carefully about how to help others. Amen."

    Session 2: Build & Present¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer & Review (3 min)¶

    Prayer: "Jesus, help us build with love today. May our creations serve others and honor You. Amen."

    Review plans: "What are you building? How will it help?"

    Building Time (17 min)¶

    Students build their designs.

    Teacher circulates:

    • "Tell me how this helps."

    • "How will you test it?"

    • "What changes are you making?"

    Encourage iteration:

    • Test as you build

    • It's okay to change your plan

    • Ask for help when needed

    Quick Testing (4 min)¶

    Test designs with a toy figure and a tabletop paper load only. Default: paper carry tray holds three crumpled paper balls for five seconds; redesign one fold and retest. Ask about user preferences rather than assuming every older/disabled person needs the same help.

    • Does it work?

    • What would make it better?

    Presentations (4 min)¶

    Quick presentations: Each group shares:

    • "We designed this for..." (who it helps)

    • "It works by..." (how it helps)

    • "We learned..." (what they discovered)

    Closing Celebration (2 min)¶

    Faith Connection: "You were Jesus's hands today! You thought about others' needs and created to help them. That's what Catholic engineers do — they use their skills to serve!"

    Closing Prayer: "Thank you, God, for minds that create and hearts that care. Help us always use our gifts to serve 'the least of these.' We want to be Your hands in the world. Amen."

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Demonstrated empathy for the user's needs

    • Created a design plan

    • Built a prototype

    • Explained how design helps others

    SAFETY / access¶

    All products are models, not real medical or assistive devices. No human lifting, body-worn restraint, blindfolding, climbing to a fountain/shelf or overhead loads. Teacher precuts cardboard, screens recyclables and limits tests to paper loads. Grade 1 orally demonstrates one feature/test; Grade 2 explains one evidence-based revision. Reserve final 4 building/planning minutes each meeting for cleanup/storage.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We were designers for others! Ask your child: 'Who did you design for?' 'How does your invention help them?' 'What would you improve?' Talk about how your family can be 'helping hands' for people in need in your community."

    Unit Version: 1.0 | Last Updated: 2025-12-05

    Week 28: Pi Day Circles¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Mathematics and design / Pi Day Circles
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, M, A
    Big idea We can compare distances around circles using the same unit.
    Student objective "I can compare two circle edges and use circles to make a repeating design."
    Why Accurate measurement and purposeful patterns matter more than memorizing digits.
    Catholic connection Honest evidence: report approximate measures without pretending they are exact; teacher application of faith/reason, CCC 159 (source below).
    Standards Local CST-C1: name measurement uncertainty; CST-M1: compare two boundaries; CST-M2: extend a repeating pattern; CST-A2: intentional form/pattern. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: paper/string directly show the mathematics. Robot art is not required and attaching a marker to a rolling Sphero is not part of this lesson.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class / supplies¶

    1. Choose two smooth round lids about 8 cm and 12 cm across (neither wider than 15 cm), so their boundaries fit the 60 cm yarn. Remove sharp metal edges. Trace a square to compare.
    2. Cut 60 cm lengths of yarn; prepare one equal-size block chain per team. Demonstrate wrapping yarn once with no overlap or stretching.
    3. Draw AB and AAB circle patterns on the board. Do not use food rewards.
    4. Per student: one sheet and crayon.
    5. Per team of 2-3: two round lids, two yarn lengths, 20 equal blocks about 2 cm wide (or 20 equal 2 cm paper squares) and scrap paper for comparing laid-out yarn. Check that the unit chain spans the longer boundary before class.
    6. Class: tape and board, circle/square examples; reusable lids/yarn.
    7. Teacher-only: scissors for precutting yarn; optional ruler to show approximation.
    Students Teams / lid pairs Yarn lengths Paper sheets
    10 4 8 10
    15 5 10 15
    20 7 14 20
    25 9 18 25

    Vocabulary / teacher background¶

    Circle = flat round shape; circumference = distance around its boundary; diameter = distance across through the center; approximate = close, not exact; repeating unit = part that repeats. Pi is a finite number about 3.14, the ratio of circumference to diameter. Its decimal representation does not terminate or repeat. Endless digits do not mean infinite magnitude. No ratio calculation is required of Grades 1-2. Misconception: every round-looking object is a flat circle. A ball is a sphere; its flat outline may look circular. If asked "Is pi as big as God?" No. Mathematics describes a finite quantity; a devotional analogy is not a mathematical or theological measurement.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Find a circle versus square. Explain Pi Day's 3/14 date briefly without digit recitation or theology claims.
    2. 4-8: Model wrapping yarn around one lid, marking the join, laying it flat and comparing to the same equal blocks.
    3. 8-18: Team members each help measure both lids. Align yarn starts; predict then compare. Grade 2 counts equal blocks, including "a little more than" if needed; Grade 1 points to longer/shorter. Repeat once to notice small measurement differences.
    4. 18-23: Each child traces circles in an intentional AB (Grade 1) or AAB/ABB (Grade 2) pattern. Partner extends it and explains the repeating unit.
    5. 23-26: Individual exit: identify the longer boundary, explain one measurement step and point to the repeating unit; say why a measure may be approximate.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / success¶

    Which yarn is longer when starts line up? What made our two attempts differ? What part of your pattern repeats? - Grade 1: correctly compare two boundaries; demonstrate lining up endpoints; create two complete AB units and predict the next circle. - Grade 2: record two approximate counts in the same units and justify comparison; create/extend three units of AAB or ABB; identify one uncertainty. - Teacher records not yet / prompted / independent for comparison, measurement method, pattern and honest uncertainty. No coding credit from circle artwork.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Slipping yarn: tape the starting end or teacher models a paper strip. No lids: use two teacher-drawn circles and paper strips; describe these as drawings. No equal blocks: use identical paper squares. Entire lesson works indoors without devices. Early finishers compare a third circle, not speed.

    SAFETY¶

    No food/treats, loose coins, sharp can lids, neck loops or strings tied to students. Precut yarn; teacher manages scissors. Accessible tabletop work only.

    Support / challenge / cleanup¶

    Support: pretraced circles, oral prompts and partner stabilization without taking the child's decision. Grade 1 responds by pointing/drawing. Challenge: Grade 2 compare around/across lengths informally; no required division. Cleanup: count reusable lids/blocks, coil yarn into bags, recycle scraps and retain each child's pattern.

    Family snippet / sources¶

    We compared circle boundaries with yarn and designed a repeating circle pattern. Catholic connection: honest measurement, including uncertainty. Ask: "How did you decide which circle was bigger around?" Optional: point out two circles in a room or picture; no materials/device required. No routine homework. Pi explanation gives definition and approximate value. CCC 159 concerns faith and science; the classroom honesty connection is an application, not an official benchmark. Ecclesiastes 3:11 may be read from a school-approved Bible; no unverified quotation is reproduced.

    grades-1-2year-alife-science

    Weeks 29-31: Growing Things¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Growth / Growing Things
    Time / domains Three 30-minute meetings at roughly weekly intervals / C, S, M
    Big idea Repeated observations show changes; unequal growth alone does not explain causes.
    Student objective "I can observe a seedling, measure the same way, and describe what changed."
    Why Growers use records and responsible care, not guesses or tallest-plant contests.
    Catholic connection Care for plants/resources, honestly report no growth too; CCC 2415. The Sower is a faith parable, not an experimental explanation.
    Standards Local CST-C3: care/resource choice; CST-S1: dated observation/question; CST-S3: seed/seedling model; CST-M1: height comparison; CST-M2: dated record/class display. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path. A teacher photo of changes is optional, not required.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20 minutes first setup plus 2-3 minutes school-day care check; 5 minutes cleanup each meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Check school seed/potting-mix allergy guidance. Select one untreated bean or radish variety; read packet depth/water guidance. No fertilizer, pesticides or edible harvest in class.
    2. Prestart two teacher backup pots 7-10 days earlier. Draw three dated backup observations if live growing conditions are unavailable; clearly identify teacher/picture data.
    3. Teacher makes drainage holes before class. Put pots in leakproof trays by a safe bright indoor window, not on a freezing sill/heater. No electrical grow light required.
    4. Mark a height baseline at the soil surface. Assign a named adult to check moisture on school days and before weekends; water when needed, not automatically daily. Keep care at school, including school breaks or arrange approved adult care.
    5. Make a three-column record: date / drawing / height. Leave "no shoot yet" distinct from a missing measurement.

    Supplies¶

    • Per student: one folded record sheet, pencil/crayon, individual roster check.
    • Per team of 2-3: one pot with drainage, two seeds, about 200 mL commercial potting mix, tray space, ruler or equal cubes; measuring tool reused.
    • Class: one small water jug, scoop, spill cloth, handwashing access, board display.
    • Teacher-only: seed packet, hole tool, backup pots, plant care log; optional plant pictures.
    Students Teams / pots Seeds plus 4 teacher backups Potting mix including 2 backup pots Student sheets
    10 4 12 1.2 L 10
    15 5 14 1.4 L 15
    20 7 18 1.8 L 20
    25 9 22 2.2 L 25

    At 25 keep materials on nine table trays. Teacher controls the water jug; no queue carrying wet pots. Rotate observer, measurer, recorder roles and still collect each child's record.

    Vocabulary / teacher background¶

    Seed = contains a young plant and stored food; germinate = begin growing; seedling = young plant; nutrient = substance needed for growth; data = recorded observations. Many seeds need water, oxygen and suitable temperature to germinate. Seedlings need light for making food, plus water/air/nutrients and support. Soil is a useful growing medium, not plant food or a universal requirement; plants can grow without soil under appropriate conditions. This is a longitudinal observation, not a controlled experiment proving needs. Misconception: an unsprouted seed means its caretaker was bad or lacked faith. If asked "Why did mine not grow?" Seed viability, temperature, water and other factors may matter; our records do not isolate the cause.

    Meeting 1: plant and predict (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Show seed/seedling; state objective and care boundary. Optional original prayer asks for careful stewardship.
    2. 4-8: Explain seed food versus seedling needs; demonstrate packet-based planting depth and soil-surface ruler baseline.
    3. 8-18: Teams scoop mix, plant two seeds, lightly water according to packet and label pot/date. Each child draws what is visible and predicts a future change orally.
    4. 18-22: Make a care log and place pots in trays; choose an adult checker. Explain that not every seed will sprout.
    5. 22-25: Individual evidence: point to seed/seedling, name one care action and one observation.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Meeting 2: observe and measure (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve pots; compare to first dated drawing, not another team's tallest plant.
    2. 4-8: Teacher models height from soil surface to top of shoot, same tool each time. Grade 1 may use equal cubes; Grade 2 nearest whole cm. Do not include pot height.
    3. 8-19: Each child measures or points to the baseline and records one observation; record "no visible shoot" truthfully. Compare own two dates. Teacher checks individuals while partners work.
    4. 19-23: Inspect moisture with teacher and update care log; discuss what we know versus what we cannot yet explain.
    5. 23-25: Optional Sower paraphrase (Matthew 13:3-9) and care reflection: plant growth is not a score for anyone's faith.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Meeting 3: communicate changes (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Recall measurement baseline and previous record.
    2. 4-13: Final measurement/drawing using same units; each student compares two dated observations.
    3. 13-19: Display one current height per team on class chart; separate "no shoot" from "not recorded." Grade 2 explains why different heights do not identify one cause.
    4. 19-23: Pairs present change/no change and a question. Keep plants at school unless a family chooses a free take-home plant; provide teacher care instead where needed.
    5. 23-25: Individual exit: show two dated observations and one responsible care decision.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Questions / success¶

    What changed since that date? Where does the ruler start? What if a seed does not sprout? Does our evidence prove why plants differ? - Grade 1: two dated drawings, correct baseline demonstration, longer/shorter/same comparison and one care action, all oral/drawn. - Grade 2: at least two dated measures in the same units and explanation of change; distinguish observation from an untested cause. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for observation, measurement, comparison and care; never grade germination success or home participation.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    No sprouts: retain genuine record and measure backup plant; do not relabel teacher data as student's. Mold: teacher removes affected pot sealed, cleans tray per school policy, supplies pictures. No bright window/no live growing allowed: use the three dated teacher drawings and equal-length paper plant models; assess reading/comparing observations, not live plant care mastery. Indoor work remains available all Minnesota winter; no outdoor planting required.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    No tasting seeds/plants/mix, unknown soil, spraying faces, standing water near electronics, student puncturing or glass pots. Wash hands. Teacher handles spill/mold and packet safety. Support: prefilled pots, picture steps, accessible table, adult scribing, thick equal blocks; nonreaders point/draw/tell. Challenge: Grade 2 use differences between two heights or propose a future fair test without claiming this one proves it.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Return tools, wipe trays/tables, put labeled pots safely back, wash hands and store records; adult checks care outside meetings. Family snippet: We kept dated plant records and compared change honestly, including no growth. Our Catholic connection was stewardship. Ask: "What did your evidence show, and what are you still wondering?" Optional: notice a plant or picture at home; no seed purchase, watering homework or device required. CCC 2415; optional Matthew 13 and 1 Corinthians 3:6 references use school-approved Bible (wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED). Seed-specific timing/depth must be verified against the selected packet; no universal sprouting deadline is promised.

    🦋 Week 33: New Life Engineering¶

    Lesson Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 30 minutes
    STREAM Focus E (Engineering), S (Science), R (Religion)

    Week 33: New Life Engineering¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Design and build a project related to new life/spring 2. Observe signs of new life in nature 3. Apply engineering design process 4. Connect science of life cycles to project

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Connect new life in nature to Jesus's Resurrection 2. Understand that Easter brings new life 3. Recognize God's power over death and darkness

    Week 33: New Life Engineering¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details¶

    Resurrection and New Life — At Easter, we celebrate Jesus rising from the dead. Spring shows us new life all around — flowers blooming, butterflies emerging, baby animals being born. Creation reflects the Resurrection!

    Scripture reference¶

    John 11:25; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching historical details¶

    St. Mary Magdalene — She was the first to see Jesus risen from the dead on Easter morning. She went from sadness to JOY when she saw that new life had conquered death.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • Pictures of spring/new life (butterflies, flowers, baby animals)

    • Building materials: paper, cardboard, pipe cleaners, pom poms

    • Scissors and tape

    • Spring nature items (optional: seeds, flowers)

    • Resurrection story visual

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)¶

    Easter Prayer: "Risen Jesus, You conquered death and brought us new life! As we see new life in spring, help us remember Your Resurrection. Alleluia! Amen."

    Signs of new life:

    • "What signs of spring do you see?"

    • List: flowers, butterflies, baby birds, green leaves, longer days

    • "After the cold and darkness of winter, new life comes!"

    Faith Connection: "Easter is like the biggest spring ever! Jesus was in the dark tomb, but He rose to new life. He's stronger than death!"

    Engineering Challenge Introduction (4 min)¶

    Today's Challenge: Build something that shows NEW LIFE

    Options: 1. Butterfly — Design a butterfly with moving wings 2. Flower — Create a flower that can "bloom" (open and close) 3. Bird Nest — Build a nest that can hold eggs 4. Anything else that shows new life in spring!

    Design criteria:

    • Shows the idea of "new life"

    • Has at least one moving or interactive part

    • Uses available materials creatively

    Design & Build (16 min)¶

    Quick plan (3 min):

    • Choose your project

    • Sketch your idea

    • List materials

    Building time (13 min): Students create their new life projects.

    Teacher prompts:

    • "How does this show new life?"

    • "What's your moving part?"

    • "What would make it better?"

    Encourage creativity:

    • There's no one right way!

    • Try different approaches

    • It's okay if it's not perfect

    Sharing & Closing (5 min)¶

    Quick share: Students show creations and explain:

    • "This shows new life because..."

    • "It moves like this..."

    Faith Connection: Spring growth can be a reminder of Easter hope, not a scientific demonstration of resurrection. A dormant plant and developing chrysalis are living, not dead and resurrected.

    Closing Prayer: "Risen Jesus, thank You for the gift of new life! Thank You for spring, for Easter, and for the promise that we will live forever with You. Help us share the joy of Your Resurrection with everyone we meet. Alleluia! Amen."

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Created a project representing new life

    • Included an interactive or moving element

    • Explained how project connects to new life theme

    • Connected spring/new life to Resurrection

    SAFETY / indoor default / evidence¶

    Use paper flowers with a folded opening petal as the default; no real eggs, animal collection, sharp wire ends or body-worn moving parts. Indoor spring pictures work in any weather. Grade 1 shows opening/closing twice and draws a change; Grade 2 explains one revision after a failed opening. Use final 3 building minutes for cleanup. Artistic symbolism does not establish biological causation.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We celebrated new life today! Your child made a project showing spring and new life. Ask them: 'How does your project show new life?' 'How is Easter like spring?' Look for signs of new life together in your neighborhood. Talk about how Jesus's Resurrection is the ultimate new life!"

    Introduction:

    • "What a year we've had!"

    • "Let's celebrate all we've learned and done together!"

    • "What was the HARDEST thing you learned?"

    • "What are you most PROUD of?"

    • "Show a saved bridge/design: what was its criterion, what did the test show, and what changed?" Children may point/draw/tell; communicate actual design evidence rather than a mastery badge.

    Station 2: Building Challenge

    Station 3: Memory Art

    Faith Connection: "God gave each of you amazing gifts — curiosity, creativity, kindness, and perseverance. You've grown so much this year! Keep exploring God's amazing world and using your gifts to serve others."

    • Creative hands that built and coded and created

    • Kind hearts that helped and shared

    • Our wonderful STREAM community

    Bless us over the summer. Help us keep learning and growing. Bring us back safe and ready for another great year. We give You all the glory for the great things we've done together. Amen!"

    • Participated in celebration activities

    • Shared a favorite memory or learning

Towers below 30 cm, no heavy loads, real candles, balloons or food treats; photos require school permissions. Reserve 3 station minutes for cleanup. Each child may show one saved test/change orally or by drawing; memories and certificates alone are not all-domain mastery.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    Thank you for your partnership this year! Continue exploring STREAM at home over the summer:

    • Build with blocks and household items

    • Observe nature and ask questions

    • Create art and make things together

    • Most importantly — wonder at God's amazing creation!

    Have a blessed summer! 🌟"

    🔄 Year A/B Rotation¶

New Grade 1 students can enter either rotation; teach/recheck picture sequences, observation and safe tool use before dependent challenges. Returning Grade 2 students need increased explanation and measured revision, not the assumption that new robot hardware is inherently harder.

If 34 taught meetings are required, locally schedule two reteach/evidence checks; do not claim those files already exist. Biweekly is 17 x 30 = 510 minutes and has less practice.

    🔬 Week 1: Welcome Back Scientists¶

    Lesson Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 30 minutes
    Curriculum Year B
    STREAM Focus S (Science), R (Religion)

    Week 1: Welcome Back Scientists¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Use observation skills to explore nature 2. Record observations through drawing and words 3. Ask scientific questions about what they observe 4. Follow classroom routines and expectations

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Express wonder at God's creation 2. Identify themselves as explorers of God's world 3. Practice thankfulness for nature

    Week 1: Welcome Back Scientists¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details¶

    Wonder at Creation — God made the world and called it "good." Scientists explore this good creation, discovering its beauty and order. When we observe nature carefully, we see God's handiwork.

    Scripture reference¶

    Psalm 19:1; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check numbering/translation in the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies¶

    St. Kateri Tekakwitha — A Native American saint who loved nature and saw God in the forests, rivers, and animals. She teaches us to find God in creation.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • Nature collection (leaves, pinecones, rocks, feathers)

    • Magnifying glasses

    • Science journals

    • Crayons/colored pencils

    • "I Wonder" chart paper

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    Gather in Circle

    "Dear God, thank You for this new year of discovery. Thank You for making such a wonderful world for us to explore. Open our eyes to see the amazing things in Your creation. Help us be good scientists who learn about Your world. Amen."

    Introduction: We Are Scientists! (5 min)¶

    What do scientists do?

    • Look carefully (OBSERVE)

    • Ask questions (WONDER)

    • Try things (EXPERIMENT)

    • Share what they learn (COMMUNICATE)

    Year B welcome:

    • "This year we'll explore God's creation in NEW ways!"

    • "We'll meet robots, build things, and discover wonders"

    • "Every week, we'll learn something amazing"

    St. Kateri connection:

    • Show image of St. Kateri

    • "She loved nature and found God everywhere"

    • "She teaches us that creation shows God's love"

    Nature Observation Activity (15 min)¶

    Observation stations (rotate every 5 min):

    Station 1: Touch & Feel

    • Various natural objects in bags

    • Feel without looking

    • Describe textures

    Station 2: Look Closely

    • Magnifying glasses

    • Examine leaves, rocks, feathers

    • What details do you notice?

    Station 3: Sorting

    • Natural objects to sort

    • By color? Size? Texture?

    • Make groups and explain why

    Wonder questions throughout:

    • "What do you notice?"

    • "What do you wonder?"

    • "Why do you think it looks like that?"

    Recording Observations (5 min)¶

    In science journals:

    • Draw ONE thing you observed

    • Write or dictate one thing you noticed

    • Write or dictate one question you have

    Closing (3 min)¶

    Share one wonder:

    • Each student shares one thing they noticed OR wondered

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for eyes to see, hands to touch, and minds to wonder. Thank You for St. Kateri who shows us how to love nature. Help us be curious scientists who see Your love in everything. Amen."

    SAFETY / access¶

    Teacher screens clean large specimens; no wild feathers, droppings, mold, unknown plants, tasting or forced mystery-bag touch. Children may look at pictures instead. Grade 1 tells/draws two details and a question; Grade 2 sorts by two evidence-based properties. Technology: None primary path. Use final 3 observation minutes for return/handwashing; retain observations, not participation alone.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We began our Year B STREAM journey today! We practiced observation skills with natural objects and learned about St. Kateri Tekakwitha, who loved nature. Ask your child: 'What did you observe today?' 'What do you wonder about?' Take a nature walk together and practice observing God's creation."

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Participated in observation stations

    • Used observation vocabulary

    • Recorded observations in journal

    • Asked wonder questions

    grades-1-2year-broboticscoding

    Weeks 2-3: Dash Robot Adventures¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Dash Robot Adventures
    Time / domains Two 30-minute meetings / C, T, M
    Big idea A program is stored instructions; driving by joystick is a different kind of input.
    Student objective "I can run a short stored program and use a test to improve it."
    Why Responsible designers predict, test and share tools fairly.
    Catholic connection Respect every partner's contribution and agency; teacher application of human dignity and solidarity, CCC 2407. People are not robots obeying a programmer.
    Standards Local CST-C2: inclusive turn-taking; CST-T1: show input/output and stop; CST-T2: order/debug code; CST-M1: compare travel to target. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Required primary path: Dash and compatible tablet with Blockly, because children execute physical robot programs. Unplugged alternative assesses sequences, not robot operation.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first setup plus manufacturer charging time; 4 minutes cleanup/meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Confirm actual loan, model, school-approved app/permissions and charging guidance. Use Blockly's official description and the installed block guide; do not assume generic Forward/Stop labels.
    2. Test a short program on the actual floor: drive forward 20 cm at low speed; turn right 90 degrees; drive forward 20 cm. Write installed block labels/settings on board and show Run/Stop.
    3. Mark 1 m dry floor bays and a paper target 20 cm ahead, clear of exits. Keep observers outside each bay.
    4. Make three picture cards and a tabletop token. Assign teams of 2-3 with programmer, observer and safety-checker roles; swap after each run.

    Supplies / scaling¶

    • Per student: half-sheet, crayon, teacher roster evidence box.
    • Per team: one charged robot/tablet kit, three cards, token, 20 cm target strip.
    • Whole class: tape, timer, soft paper target, whiteboard; no obstacle course needed.
    • Teacher-only: chargers and installed app guide; cords stay stored during class.
    Students Teams / kits for simultaneous practice Papers
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    At 25 use one supervised station with three 4-minute waves of three teams if only three kits exist; other teams rehearse with cards. If only one kit exists, teacher demonstration plus limited turns is partial device assessment: record children awaiting a turn, not universal mastery. Reduce moving robots to what the adult can safely supervise.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Input = our instructions; output = movement/light; sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; debug = find/change a mismatch; distance = how far. Blockly executes connected blocks. Manual Go control is not evidence of writing stored code. A robot may veer due to floor/charge; distinguish this from a wrong block. Misconception: coding success is driving fastest. Accuracy and explanation matter. If asked "Does God program us?" No. People make meaningful choices; this lesson's Catholic connection is responsibility and inclusion, not mechanical obedience.

    Meeting 1 (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3: State safe stop signal and sharing objective. Optional original prayer: "God, help us include every partner and learn honestly from our tests."
    2. 3-7: Predict a tabletop three-card sequence; each child moves token once.
    3. 7-11: Teacher shows stored Blockly program and contrasts with manual driving; demonstrate Run and Stop before student use.
    4. 11-23: Teams execute tested short programs. Each child predicts, runs/stops and compares ending to target; swap roles. Grade 1 may begin with forward plus light; Grade 2 adds the turn/second movement.
    5. 23-26: Individual oral/drawn exit: show input and output; order cards matching own run. Teacher records actual device participation.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Meeting 2 (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Recall the previous run; new entrants rehearse two cards rather than needing Year A.
    2. 4-8: Teacher deliberately makes the first movement too short; model prediction, observation and one distance change.
    3. 8-20: Each child changes one block/parameter, reruns and compares to target. Grade 2 describes nearer/farther before and after; no automatic maze completion or expertise claim.
    4. 20-24: Pairs show original versus changed sequence and explain output. Optional finite repeat of a light/wait sequence for ready Grade 2 children.
    5. 24-26: Individual evidence check and remaining-turn roster.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / measurable success¶

    What is stored before you press Run? How is this different from driving? Which instruction caused a change? How did your group include everyone? - Grade 1: point to/orally order two actions, personally start/stop one stored run with supervision, show a change and one equitable turn choice. - Grade 2: build/order three actions, predict the ending, change one instruction and explain observed improvement using nearer/farther or measured distance. - Record 0 not observed / 1 prompted / 2 independent for each child's sequence, device operation, debug and inclusion. No credit for a teammate's run.

    If things go wrong / no-device and indoor fallback¶

    Connection: check correct robot and charge once; switch after two minutes, explicitly noting unassessed device skills. Token fallback uses the same prediction/change sequence; assess CST-T2 only, not Dash programming/operation mastery. Veering: stop and lower speed/shorten path on a flat surface. All work is indoors; no weather dependency.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Low-speed dry floor bays only; stop if robot crosses boundary. Never chase, race, ride or hold a running robot. Teacher handles charging/cables. Safe accessible tabletop token alternative is available without stigmatizing a child. Support: picture cards, narration, adult scribing, two actions and large buttons; nonreaders never copy typed directions. Challenge: Grade 2 explains two trials or a finite light loop, not sensors/autonomous navigation.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Stop, save only to school-controlled device as permitted, power down, count kits/cards, clear lesson tape and return to labeled trays; teacher charges. Family snippet: We predicted and debugged stored robot instructions and shared turns respectfully. Ask: "What input changed the robot's output?" Optional: move a paper token with three spoken instructions; no device or purchase. No routine homework. Blockly official app; CCC 2407. Solanus Casey biography is optional and VERIFICATION REQUIRED before use; it is not needed to assess patience.

    grades-1-2year-bsciencearts

    Week 4: Senses and Discovery¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Observation / Senses and Discovery
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, A
    Big idea Different safe tools/senses reveal different details; everyone can contribute evidence.
    Student objective "I can describe two details and compare two objects using a safe way to observe."
    Why Observations support comparisons without requiring every child to use every sense.
    Catholic connection Respect dignity and access; do not compare a child's body to another as better/worse. Teacher application of CCC 2407.
    Standards Local CST-C2: choose an inclusive observation method; CST-S1: describe two details; CST-A1: sketch observed detail; CST-M2: sort by a stated property. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: direct observation suffices.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class¶

    1. Screen clean large textured objects: cloth, smooth plastic lid and corrugated cardboard. Remove scents, food, feathers, spices and unknown plant materials.
    2. Teacher seals two identical rice shakers permanently, checks leakage and never opens them in class. Alternative: teacher claps two gentle sound patterns; children can observe motion instead of listening.
    3. Put texture examples and two lids of visibly different sizes at each table. Draw a two-box observation sheet on the board; folding plain paper suffices.
    4. Offer look, safe optional touch, or picture/tactile replica; never surprise-touch or blindfold a child. Show quiet space and opt-out choices.

    Supplies¶

    • Per student: one folded sheet, crayon.
    • Per team of 2-3: three large clean texture examples, two smooth lids; optional plastic magnifier.
    • Whole class: two permanently sealed shakers, timer, sorting mat, handwashing.
    • Teacher-only: shaker sealing/checking, roster, object screening; no taste/smell supplies.
    Students Teams / texture sets Papers
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    At 25 use table work plus one teacher sound demo; no five-station traffic or shared mouth instruments.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Observe = notice safely; texture = surface feel or appearance; compare = describe what is alike/different; evidence = noticed detail; sort = group by a property. Sight/hearing/touch are options, not requirements. Scientists use instruments when direct senses are unavailable or unsafe. Tasting an unknown substance is never a scientific observation method for this class. Misconception: a guessing game answer matters more than evidence. "Bumpy ridges" is better evidence than "I think it is a shell." If asked "Why aren't we tasting?" Taste can expose allergens/unsafe substances; today's objectives need no food.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: State objective, access choices and safe touch rule; optional original prayer thanks God for each person's contributions.
    2. 4-8: Teacher models two details on cardboard using looking and optional touch; contrast observation with guess.
    3. 8-17: Teams examine texture examples; each child draws/points/describes two details. Partner compares two objects using rough/smooth, size or visible ridges. Teacher checks individuals.
    4. 17-21: Teacher demonstrates quiet sealed shaker sounds or gentle claps with visible movement. Children compare patterns by hearing or seeing; no requirement to hear.
    5. 21-26: Each child sorts two objects by one stated property and explains/draws evidence. Grade 2 sorts same objects a second way. Partners name a method that includes someone who chooses not to touch/hear.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup and handwashing.

    Questions / success¶

    What did you notice rather than guess? Which observation method is safe for you? Can the same objects be grouped another way? - Grade 1: oral/pointed/drawn two details, one alike/different comparison and one grouping reason; choose an accessible method. - Grade 2: two precise details, two defensible grouping rules and an explanation that a different method can still supply evidence. - Teacher marks not yet / prompted / independent for details, sorting and inclusion; never scores use of all senses.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Leaking shaker: remove immediately and use claps/visible motion. Sensory overload: quiet visual/tactile table by choice. Missing objects: use large teacher drawings with visible texture marks; distinguish pictured observations from touch evidence. Entire lesson is indoors and no-device ready.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    No tasting, smell jars, blindfolds, reaching into unknown bags, loud shaking near ears, loose beans/rice or forced touch. Teacher seals and counts shakers. Respect sensory and physical access without implying anyone is less blessed. Support: two picture choices, sentence starter "I notice...", oral response, larger objects and adult scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 justify two classifications or ask what a magnifier might reveal.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Return/count objects, wipe washable surfaces per school practice, recycle scraps and wash hands. Family snippet: We compared details using safe accessible observation methods. Our Catholic connection was including every observer. Ask: "What detail helped you sort an object?" Optional: describe a familiar object or picture together; no tasting or purchase. No routine homework. CCC 2407; Psalm 139:14 is an optional reference in a school-approved Bible, not an unverified quotation. Isidore's specific sensory practices are not historical evidence and are omitted.

    grades-1-2year-bengineeringlightservicearts

    🗼 Weeks 5-6: Tower Engineering¶

    Unit Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 2 sessions (30 min each)
    Curriculum Year B
    STREAM Focus E (Engineering), M (Math), S (Science)

    Weeks 5-6: Tower Engineering¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Apply engineering design process to build tall structures 2. Explore concepts of balance, stability, and height 3. Measure height using non-standard and standard units 4. Test, iterate, and improve designs

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Connect towers to the Tower of Babel story 2. Understand the difference between prideful building and serving others 3. Work cooperatively as a team

    Weeks 5-6: Tower Engineering¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED¶

    Genesis 11 is a theological story to read from an approved source, not a guarantee that a faithful engineer's structure succeeds. Good engineers learn from failed models and can serve others without a winning tower.

    Scripture reference¶

    Psalm 127:1; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies¶

    St. Joseph the Worker — Patron of workers and craftsmen. He built things with his hands to provide for his family and serve others, not for pride.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • KEVA planks (large supply)

    • Measuring tools (rulers, non-standard units)

    • Recording sheets

    • Images of famous towers

    • Building area with crash zones

    Session 1: Tower Basics¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "Dear God, help us be good builders today. Not builders who are proud, but builders who work together and help others. Bless our hands and minds as we create. Amen."

    Introduction: Famous Towers (5 min)¶

    Show images:

    • Leaning Tower of Pisa

    • Eiffel Tower

    • Church steeples

    • Lighthouse towers

    Discussion:

    • "Why do people build towers?"

    • "What makes a tower stay up?"

    • "What makes a tower fall down?"

    Tower of Babel connection:

    • Tell brief story: People built a tower to make themselves famous

    • "God wants us to build to SERVE others, not to brag"

    • "Today we'll build towers to learn engineering!"

    Engineering Investigation (8 min)¶

    Key concepts:

    Base:

    • Wider base = more stable

    • Demonstrate: One block base vs. four blocks base

    Balance:

    • Weight must be even

    • Show: Unbalanced tower falls

    Height:

    • Higher = harder to balance

    • Each level adds challenge

    Let students explore:

    • What happens with different base sizes?

    • What happens when you add weight on top?

    Build Challenge Round 1 (12 min)¶

    Challenge: Build the TALLEST tower you can!

    Rules:

    • KEVA planks only

    • Must stand for 10 seconds

    • Work in partners

    • Stay in your area

    Teacher circulates:

    • "How tall is your tower?"

    • "What happens when you add more?"

    • "Why do you think it fell?"

    Measure towers:

    • Use hand spans or rulers

    • Record heights

    Closing (3 min)¶

    Quick share:

    • What worked?

    • What made towers fall?

    Preview: "Next time: even TALLER towers!"

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for teaching us about building. Help us use what we learn to help others. Amen."

    Session 2: Tower Challenge¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "St. Joseph, you worked with your hands to serve your family. Help us work well today to build and learn. Amen."

    Review & Strategy (5 min)¶

    What we learned:

    • Wide bases help

    • Balance matters

    • Adding slowly works better

    New strategies:

    • Cross-patterns for stability

    • Layer building

    • Checking balance before adding

    Challenge announcement:

    • "Today: tallest tower that can hold a small weight on top!"

    • Added difficulty: Must support a small object

    Tower Engineering Challenge (18 min)¶

    Phase 1: Build (12 min)

    • Partners work together

    • Build tallest stable tower

    • Prepare to add weight

    Phase 2: Test (6 min)

    • Add small weight to top (eraser, small ball)

    • Must stand for 10 seconds with weight

    • Measure final height

    Recording:

    • Tower height (in hand spans or inches)

    • Did it hold the weight?

    • Draw your tower design

    Data Sharing (3 min)¶

    Class comparison:

    • Which tower was tallest?

    • Which held weight the best?

    • What designs worked well?

    Key discoveries:

    • What patterns do we see in successful towers?

    Closing (2 min)¶

    Faith connection: "St. Joseph built good, strong things for his family. The best builders don't build to show off — they build to help others. How could engineers use tower-building to help people?" (Lighthouses, communication towers, church steeples)

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for engineers who build things that help people. Help us use our building skills for good. Amen."

    SAFETY / evidence / cleanup¶

    Tabletop tower height maximum 30 cm, soft eraser load only, never a ball/book/heavy weight. Clear hands/faces for 10-second tests; no climbing or catching a collapse. Replace "even taller" goal with same-height stability comparison. Grade 1 points to base and compares two tests; Grade 2 records height in the same units before/after one redesign. Last 4 building minutes each meeting are tool count/storage/cleanup. Technology: None primary path.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We engineered towers this week! Ask your child: 'What makes a tower stable?' 'What was your tallest tower?' 'What did you learn when it fell?' We discussed building for service vs. pride (Tower of Babel). Try building towers at home with blocks, cards, or household items!"

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Applied engineering concepts (base, balance)

    • Measured tower height

    • Iterated on design after failures

    • Worked cooperatively with partner

    🐾 Weeks 7-9: Animal Habitats¶

    Unit Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 3 sessions (30 min each)
    Curriculum Year B
    STREAM Focus S (Science), E (Engineering), R (Religion)

    Weeks 7-9: Animal Habitats¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Identify what animals need to survive (food, water, shelter) 2. Research a specific animal's habitat needs 3. Design and build a model habitat 4. Explain how their habitat meets the animal's needs

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Understand stewardship of animals as God's command 2. Show care for creatures as part of creation 3. Connect habitat care to environmental responsibility

    Weeks 7-9: Animal Habitats¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details¶

    Stewardship of Creation — God gave humans responsibility to care for animals and the earth. Designing habitats helps us understand what animals need so we can protect them.

    Scripture reference¶

    Genesis 2:15; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies¶

    St. Francis of Assisi — Patron of animals who called creatures his brothers and sisters. He teaches us to respect and care for all living things.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • Animal picture cards

    • Habitat research books/materials

    • Building materials (boxes, paper, natural items)

    • Craft supplies

    • Habitat planning sheets

    • Model animal toys

    Session 1: Animal Needs¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "St. Francis, you loved all animals as brothers and sisters. Help us learn about animals today so we can care for them better. Teach us to be good stewards of God's creatures. Amen."

    Introduction: What Animals Need (8 min)¶

    All animals need:

    • 🍎 Food — What do they eat?

    • 💧 Water — Where do they find water?

    • 🏠 Shelter — Where do they live? What protects them?

    • 🌡️ Right conditions — Temperature, light, space

    A HABITAT provides these things!

    Examples:

    • Fish: Water, water plants, pond or tank

    • Bird: Seeds, water dish, trees or birdhouse

    • Rabbit: Vegetables, water, burrow or hutch

    St. Francis connection:

    • "He called the sun 'Brother Sun' and the moon 'Sister Moon'"

    • "All creatures are our family"

    • "We take care of family!"

    Animal Research (15 min)¶

    Choose an animal to research:

    • Bird (robin, cardinal, owl)

    • Mammal (rabbit, squirrel, deer)

    • Insect (butterfly, bee, ladybug)

    • Reptile (turtle); amphibian (frog)

    Research questions: 1. What does your animal EAT? 2. What does your animal DRINK? 3. Where does your animal LIVE? 4. What keeps your animal SAFE? 5. Does it need special temperature or space?

    Record on planning sheet:

    • Draw the animal

    • List what it needs

    • Draw where it lives

    Closing (5 min)¶

    Share findings:

    • What animal did you research?

    • What's ONE thing it needs?

    Preview: "Next time: design your habitat!"

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for all the animals You created. Help us be good caretakers of Your creatures. Amen."

    Session 2: Habitat Design¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "Creator God, help us design good homes for animals today. May our work show love for Your creatures. Amen."

    Design Phase (10 min)¶

    Review animal needs from research.

    Design questions:

    • How will you show where the animal gets FOOD?

    • How will you show where it gets WATER?

    • Where is the SHELTER?

    • How is it PROTECTED?

    Draw your habitat design:

    • Bird's eye view (from above)

    • Label the parts

    • List materials you'll need

    Teacher approval before building.

    Building Phase (15 min)¶

    Available materials:

    • Cardboard boxes (various sizes)

    • Construction paper

    • Natural items (sticks, leaves, rocks)

    • Cotton balls, fabric scraps

    • Glue, tape, scissors

    Build your habitat!

    • Include ALL four things animal needs

    • Make it appropriate size (model)

    • Be creative!

    Teacher circulates:

    • "Where does the animal get food?"

    • "Where is the water?"

    • "Where does it shelter?"

    • "How did you protect it?"

    Closing (3 min)¶

    Quick share:

    • Show your progress

    • What's working well?

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You for time to create today. Bless our habitats and help us finish them well. Amen."

    Session 3: Habitat Presentations¶

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "St. Francis, help us share what we've learned about caring for animals. May we always treat creatures with kindness. Amen."

    Finishing Touches (8 min)¶

    Complete habitats:

    • Final additions

    • Labels if desired

    • Prepare to present

    Habitat Presentations (15 min)¶

    Each student shares with a partner or a table group; teacher samples every individual's needs explanation at tables. At 25 students, do not promise 25 full-class presentations in 15 minutes. 1. "My animal is ___________." 2. "Here is where it gets FOOD: ___________." 3. "Here is where it gets WATER: ___________." 4. "Here is its SHELTER: ___________." 5. "I protect it by ___________."

    Audience response:

    • One thing you like about this habitat

    • One question

    Real-World Connection (3 min)¶

    Discussion:

    • "How can we help REAL animals have good habitats?"

    • Bird feeders

    • Bee-friendly gardens

    • Not disturbing wild areas

    • Clean water

    Stewardship commitment:

    • "God gave us responsibility for animals"

    • "What's ONE thing you could do to help animals?"

    Closing (2 min)¶

    Celebration:

    • "You are habitat engineers!"

    • "You learned to think about what animals need"

    • "You can use this to help real animals"

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for trusting us to care for Your animals. Help us be good stewards of all creatures. May we always remember that animals are our brothers and sisters in creation. Amen."

    SAFETY / habitat accuracy / evidence¶

    Models only: no live animal housing, wildlife collecting, nest disturbance or unapproved bird-feeder deployment. Teacher provides vetted species pictures/books; generic food examples are not care instructions for every species. Screen natural/recycled items; no sharp staples/glass. Grade 1 points to three species-specific needs orally; Grade 2 explains a condition/space choice and a model limitation. Use final 4 making minutes each meeting for cleanup. Technology: None primary path; printed/teacher-read species sources replace independent internet research.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We designed animal habitats! Ask your child: 'What animal did you research?' 'What four things do animals need?' 'How did you include them in your habitat?' We learned about St. Francis and caring for creation. Consider putting up a bird feeder or planting flowers for bees as a family stewardship project!"

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Identified four animal needs

    • Researched specific animal requirements

    • Designed habitat addressing all needs

    • Presented and explained habitat

    Week 10: Ramp Races¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Motion / Ramp Races: compare rather than race
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, M
    Big idea Changing one test condition and keeping others alike helps us compare results.
    Student objective "I can release the same car without a push and compare its stopping distances."
    Why Evidence, repeated tests and honest records are useful beyond competition.
    Catholic connection Honest evidence and respect for others' results; teacher application of faith/reason, CCC 159. Physical laws are not the moral meaning of Catholic natural law.
    Standards Local CST-C1: distinguish data/guess; CST-S2: keep fair-test conditions; CST-S3: gravity/motion model; CST-M1: measure distance; CST-M2: two-condition results. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: direct measurement; no speed sensor or video needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class / supplies¶

    1. Test a 40-50 cm rigid cardboard ramp with one and two thin books, maximum support height 10 cm. Tape securely in a shallow tray/table lane with end catch box; runout cannot enter an aisle.
    2. Mark fixed starting point and ramp-end line. Use same toy car, ramp, lane and release method for both heights. Do not change cars or landing surfaces during this test.
    3. Prepare two-column low/high recording paper; teacher makes a shared example.
    4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, personal prediction.
    5. Per team of 2-3: one car, ramp, two books, tape, measuring strip of equal 2 cm marks or equal cubes, catch box.
    6. Class: timer, class chart; reusable kits.
    7. Teacher-only: ramp preflight, height check, roster. No small loose balls or launched loads.
    Students Teams / complete ramp kits Individual sheets
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    At 25 use nine parallel table lanes only if table area contains each run. Otherwise three supervised lanes with three 4-minute waves; off-lane teams predict and compare teacher example data. Record any student not observed releasing/measuring.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Gravity = Earth's pull on objects; distance = how far; trial = one test; condition = test setting; fair test = keep important things the same except the planned change. At these small classroom heights gravity is effectively unchanged. A higher starting position can provide more gravitational potential energy. Runout depends on ramp/surface/car; farther stopping distance does not measure speed directly, and results may differ. Misconception: gravity pulls harder from a higher ramp. It does not in this setup. If asked "Which car was faster?" We measured stopping distance, not time/speed; that needs a different test.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3: Explain comparison objective and lane rule; each child predicts low/high/same by pointing.
    2. 3-7: Model no-push release and measuring from ramp end to car's final front position; count equal units, always same reference.
    3. 7-10: Identify what stays the same and changed book height; pairs rehearse roles: releaser, measurer, recorder.
    4. 10-22: Run three low and three high trials per team, swapping roles. Record each result, including surprises; Grade 1 uses marks/cubes, Grade 2 whole cm if ready. Do not force a predicted pattern.
    5. 22-26: Each child points to one result for each condition, compares, and names one controlled feature; ask whether the trials agree.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / measurable evidence¶

    Did you push? Where does measurement start? What changed? Does one result prove a rule for every car? - Grade 1: release without push, compare one low/high result orally or with drawn lengths, name same car/start. - Grade 2: record at least two trials per condition, compare spread/typical result informally, name one changed and two unchanged features; no required averages. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for release, measurement and evidence-based comparison. Winning a race is not assessed.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Car leaves lane: stop, lower ramp and add catch sides. Car does not roll: inspect wheels/ramp join and retest at same low setting; document change. Inconsistent results are valid; revisit release and surface. No kits: teacher demonstrates while children compare honest shared results, noting direct manipulation not individually assessed. Indoors year-round, no devices needed.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Ramp below 10 cm; gentle releases only; cars not projectiles. No heavy loads, standing on furniture, chasing or lanes across routes. Teacher approves stable supports. Support: prebuilt lane, two trials per condition with scaffolded comparison, tactile equal-unit strip, scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 proposes a later different-surface test while explaining why not to combine changes today.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Park/count cars, detach only lesson tape, stack books/ramps, store data. We tested ramp heights and compared measured stopping distances with honest records. Ask: "What did you keep the same?" Optional: describe a ramp seen in a picture or school; no home experiment required. No routine homework. CCC 159. Physics explanation uses standard elementary mechanics; official benchmark alignment remains VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Albert the Great biography is optional and must be verified before adding.

    🦃 Week 11: Thanksgiving Coding¶

    Lesson Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 30 minutes
    Curriculum Year B
    STREAM Focus T (Technology), R (Religion), A (Arts)

    Week 11: Thanksgiving Coding¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Create a ScratchJr project with multiple characters 2. Use speech bubbles to express ideas 3. Sequence events in a simple animation 4. Add backgrounds and personalize projects

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Express gratitude through digital creation 2. Identify things they're thankful for 3. Connect gratitude to prayer

    Week 11: Thanksgiving Coding¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection¶

    Thanksgiving is a form of prayer; CCC 2637-2638. Do not present a four-item classroom mnemonic as the Catechism's exhaustive classification.

    Scripture reference¶

    Psalm 107:1; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies¶

    St. Thérèse of Lisieux — Found joy in small things and was constantly grateful. Her "Little Way" teaches us to thank God for everyday blessings.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • iPads with ScratchJr

    • Thankful brainstorm sheets

    • Sample project to show

    • Thanksgiving-themed stickers (optional)

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "Dear God, thank You! Thank You for families, food, friends, and fun. Thank You for this school and for each other. Help us create projects today that show our gratitude. Amen."

    Introduction: Gratitude Coding (5 min)¶

    What are you thankful for?

    • Quick brainstorm: family, pets, food, home, friends, toys, nature

    • "St. Thérèse was thankful for even SMALL things"

    • The specific attributed "flowers" saying is unverified; omit it. Children can express their own gratitude without an attributed quote.

    Today's project:

    • Create a "Thank You" animation

    • Characters will SAY what they're thankful for

    • Make it colorful and joyful!

    Show sample project:

    • Character with speech bubble

    • "I'm thankful for my family!"

    • Another character appears

    • "I'm thankful for my dog!"

    Planning (3 min)¶

    Think about YOUR project: 1. What are 2-3 things you're thankful for? 2. What characters will say these things? 3. What background fits?

    Quick sketch:

    • Draw your thankful things

    • Note which character says which thing

    ScratchJr Creation (17 min)¶

    Step-by-step guidance:

    Step 1: Choose background

    • Find a thankful scene

    • Home, nature, table scene

    Step 2: Add character

    • Choose a person, animal, or object

    • Place on screen

    Step 3: Add speech

    • Find speech bubble block

    • Type "I'm thankful for ___________!"

    • Add wait time

    Step 4: Add more!

    • Another character?

    • Another thankful thing?

    • Movement or animation?

    Stretch challenges:

    • Character moves across screen

    • Two characters have a conversation

    • Add sound effects

    • Multiple scenes

    Teacher circulates:

    • Help with technical issues

    • Ask "What are you thankful for?"

    • Encourage creativity

    Sharing (3 min)¶

    Quick gallery walk or partner share:

    • Show your neighbor your project

    • Tell them what you're thankful for

    Celebration:

    • "You coded your GRATITUDE!"

    • "You can share this with your family"

    Closing (2 min)¶

    St. Thérèse connection:

    • "She found joy in tiny blessings"

    • "What 'small thing' are you thankful for?"

    • "Gratitude is a kind of PRAYER!"

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for EVERYTHING — big and small. Thank You for the creativity to make projects that share our gratitude. Help us be thankful people every day, not just at Thanksgiving. Amen."

    Technology / nonreader / privacy¶

    Required primary path: school-approved ScratchJr tablets for executed code. Grade 1 dictates or records a short message instead of typing; demonstrate green-flag plus two ordered actions. Grade 2 changes one action and explains output. No devices: paper panels and oral sequence/debug; no app-operation/executed-program mastery claim. Do not upload names/photos/voices outside approved storage. Use final 3 creation minutes for save/return/cleanup. Optional home discussion needs no tablet.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We created gratitude animations in ScratchJr! Ask your child to show you their project. Ask: 'What are you thankful for?' We learned that gratitude is a form of prayer. At dinner this week, go around and share something each person is thankful for."

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Created ScratchJr project with character(s)

    • Used speech bubbles to express gratitude

    • Identified multiple things to be thankful for

    • Connected gratitude to prayer

    🎁 Week 12: Gifts for Others¶

    Lesson Overview¶
    Grade Level Grades 1-2
    Duration 30 minutes
    Curriculum Year B
    STREAM Focus E (Engineering), A (Arts), R (Religion)

    Week 12: Gifts for Others¶

    🎯 Learning Objectives¶

    STEM Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Design with a user in mind 2. Use materials purposefully 3. Follow design constraints 4. Create a functional item

    Faith Integration Objectives¶

    Students will be able to: 1. Practice generosity through making 2. Understand that gifts of time and effort are meaningful 3. Think of others' needs before their own

    Week 12: Gifts for Others¶

    🙏 Faith-Reason Integration¶

    Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details¶

    Gift of Self — The best gifts are those that give of ourselves — our time, effort, and love. Handmade gifts show we value the person enough to invest ourselves.

    Scripture reference¶

    2 Corinthians 9:7; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

    Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies/traditions¶

    St. Nicholas — Famous for giving gifts in secret. He gave to those in need without expecting anything in return. He inspires our gift-giving at Christmas.

    📚 Materials Needed¶

    • Cardstock/construction paper

    • Craft sticks

    • Beads, buttons

    • Glue, tape, scissors

    • Markers, crayons

    • Gift-making templates (optional)

    • Brown paper for wrapping

    📝 Lesson Procedure (30 minutes)¶

    Opening Prayer (2 min)¶

    "Dear God, help us be cheerful givers today. As we make gifts for others, fill us with love. Help us think about what would make someone else happy. Amen."

    Introduction: Giving Gifts (4 min)¶

    St. Nicholas story:

    • "He gave gifts to people in need"

    • "He gave SECRETLY — didn't want thanks"

    • "He shows us how to be generous"

    Handmade gifts are special:

    • "When you MAKE something, you give your TIME"

    • "That's more valuable than money!"

    • "Thinking about what someone else wants = LOVE"

    Today's challenge:

    • Make a gift for someone you care about

    • Think: What would THEY like?

    • Not what YOU like — what THEY like!

    Planning Phase (5 min)¶

    Think about your recipient:

    • Who will you give this to?

    • What do they like?

    • What colors do they enjoy?

    • What would make them smile?

    Choose your project:

    Option A: Bookmark

    • For someone who reads

    • Personalize with colors they like

    Option B: Picture Frame

    • Made from craft sticks

    • Decorate for them

    • They can add a photo

    Option C: Decoration

    • Ornament or hanging art

    • For their room or tree

    Option D: Card with Art

    • Special handmade card

    • Include a drawing for them

    Making Phase (15 min)¶

    Create your gift!

    Design thinking reminders:

    • "Is this what THEY would like?"

    • "Are you using THEIR favorite colors?"

    • "Would this make THEM smile?"

    Craftsmanship matters:

    • Take your time

    • Do your best work

    • This shows you care!

    Teacher circulates:

    • "Who is this for?"

    • "What do they like about it?"

    • "How will they use it?"

    Closing (4 min)¶

    Wrap it up:

    • Simple wrapping if time allows

    • Write "To: ___" and "From: ___"

    Sharing:

    • "Who is your gift for?"

    • "What did you think about while making it?"

    St. Nicholas connection:

    • "He gave without wanting thanks"

    • "Can you give this gift and not brag about it?"

    • "Let the GIFT show your love, not your words"

    Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for people we love. Thank You for the ability to make things with our hands. Help us be cheerful givers like St. Nicholas. May our gifts bring joy to others. Amen."

    SAFETY / workable default¶

    Use a 5 x 15 cm teacher-precut cardstock bookmark; choose recipient, draw a purposeful message/pattern, test in a closed book and revise anything that obstructs use. Omit loose beads/buttons, hot glue and staples. Grade 1 dictates; Grade 2 explains one design revision. Technology: None primary path. Final 3 making minutes are cleanup; functional testing, not decoration alone, supports engineering evidence.

    📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)¶

    "We made gifts with a recipient in mind. Ask: 'What did you choose for that person, and why?' Handmade, purchased and spoken gifts can all express love; do not rank families by purchases or time available."

    ✅ Assessment¶

    • Designed with recipient in mind

    • Created thoughtful, careful work

    • Considered what recipient would enjoy

    • Connected gift-making to generosity
